Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to make submissions on this issue. I would like to begin by making some general observations and then proceed to indicate my specific concerns on the Meech Lake Accord.
A constitution is a body of fundamental principles according to which a state is governed. Changes to a state's constitution, as Machiavelli once advised, must be made with the utmost care.
In my view the Constitutional Accord signed by the First Ministers is not in the best interests of Canada or Canadians. It does not accurately reflect what Canada is or what it ought to be. It does not reflect in my view what I consider to be the views and aspirations of a majority of Canadians. The Accord, if enacted with its present provisions, will result in a weaker federal Government. It will set in motion a series of changes which, over time, will render the federal Government irrelevant.
Quebec's participation in the Constitution is essential. Nevertheless at some point we have to ask ourselves whether the price of obtaining Quebec's unconditional approval of the Constitution is too high for the Confederation as a whole. In my view, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Premiers went too far in order to gain Quebec's participation. In the "real politik" of federal-provincial negotiations, Premiers cannot be faulted for negotiating on their own particular agendas. They have electorates to satisfy, constituencies to placate and political objectives to obtain.
It is the role of the Prime Minister in this process to ensure that, while every reasonable effort is made to accommodate provincial aspirations, the federal Parliament retains the power to enact and act in the national interest. The Prime Minister must ensure that Parliament has the power to set national standards and objectives for important social and economic programs, to assist smaller less advantaged provinces and to speak clearly for Canada in foreign affairs.
Of course, in a vast and diverse country such as Canada, a certain amount of decentralization is both healthy and inevitable. Federalism was and is the only system of government able to accommodate the distinct character of each province and the rich diversity which makes Canada unique among nations. The Fathers of Confederation recognized this
fact in drafting the British North America Act and it is as true now as it was then. Canadian federalism has always been characterized by a healthy tension, a fine balancing act between central and provincial power.
In some respects, the debate over the recent constitutional Accord has become obscured by the simplistic notion that somehow we are debating a polarized vision of whether Canada should be a highly centralized or decentralized federal structure. In fact, Canada is already a highly decentralized federation.
The debate on the Accord, if it is to reflect reality, must centre on whether or not we wish to tip the delicate balance considerably further with respect to an even more decentralized federalism with fewer constitutional powers for the central Government and weaker national institutions. To appreciate how decentralized our federation has become, one only need examine the trends with respect to who spends the money.
Between 1968 and fiscal year 1987-88, the total amount of transfer payments made to the provinces by the federal Government rose from $2.8 billion to $29.8 billion. This represents a real increase of well over 100 per cent even if one takes into account inflation.
In addition, the federal Government's share of public revenues in Canada decreased from 47 per cent to 37 per cent between 1962 and 1986. In the same period the provinces, and municipalities, share rose from 53 per cent to 63 per cent, from just over one-half to almost two-thirds of all public revenue.
From a fiscal standpoint, Canada ranks with Switzerland as one of the most decentralized federations in the world. Given, the ascendancy of provincial power over the last 25 years, it is now time for Canadians to ask themselves whether we wish first, to push the pendulum even further toward more provincial authority and even greater decentralization, second, to maintain the status quo; or third, to seek to reassert federal authority. The constitutional debate will afford Canadians an opportunity to articulate their vision, their view and their dream of what Canada should be.
We already know the views of one prominent Canadian who has spoken out many times on the subject of Canadian federalism. In 1984, former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau warned Canadians that:
With too much decentralization in the name of cultural security and
provincial autonomy, the country risks fragmentation and disorderly
competition in a world where, to an increasing extent, only the strongest and
most disciplined can survive and prosper.
This is the crux of the issue. At the very least, federal power must be maintained to allow the federal Government to pursue national, social and economic objectives. Living in today's world economy has become in a very real sense survival of the fittest. The Japanese, the South Koreans and the West Germans, with their integrated and disciplined economies, have achieved a competitive edge in world trade based on cohesive national strategies. be measured in their huge trade surpluses has been marked by a national unity of purpose and a commitment to foster economic excellence in certain sectors of world markets. Important political decisions have been made in these countries not to support industries which cannot compete.
How does all this relate to the present constitutional Accord? I see the Accord as the thin edge of a large wedge with which the provinces can and will acquire more power to pursue their own economic, social and even political objectives, irrespective of any larger national purpose. The dangers of fragmentation and disorderly competition against which Mr. Trudeau warned three years ago are now coming to pass, albeit gradually. Like some constitutional Trojan horse that has been pushed inside our gates by the Prime Minister and the Premiers, the Accord looks good but its contents will cause no end of trouble in the years ahead.
Traditionally, the Liberal Party has always stood for a strong Canada in which Parliament has the necessary powers and jurisdiction to formulate public policy. Indeed, the Liberal Party in the 20th century has been one of the greatest nationbuilding institutions in Canada. We have consistently rejected concepts of special status, deux nations and the community of communities or any other doctrine which would weaken Canada.
At this juncture, I sincerely believe that it is the role of the Liberal Party to lead the way in ensuring that everything for which we have stood and fought over the years is not signed away with the stroke of a pen. Those Liberals who do not support the Accord have an obligation and indeed a duty to make their views known.
I have a number of specific concerns. Over the last number of months, prominent Canadians have expressed concerns with respect to particular provisions in the constitutional Accord. My concerns particularly relate to the clause dealing with a distinct society, the effect the constitutional Accord will have on the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the clause which deals with Senate appointments, the clause which deals with appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada, the clause dealing with spending power, the amending formula which would require unanimity on certain matters in the Constitution, and finally, my main concern deals with immigration.
Regarding my first concern, I have asked myself, as have many Canadians, why it is necessary to give special status to Quebec. There are those who argue that Clause 2(1)(a) of the constitutional Accord is simply an articulation of today's reality, the status quo in Quebec. If that is the case, why is it necessary to recognize that in the Constitution?
There are those who argue that this particular clause will give some special constitutional power to Quebec. I suppose if this Accord is ratified by the federal Parliament and the by the provincial legislatures, ultimately it will be left up to the
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Supreme Court of Canada to decide what is meant by the distinct society clause.
Even though I fail to understand why it is necessary to have recognition of Quebec as a distinct society in the Accord, my concern is over what is excluded by this clause which reads as follows:
The Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with
(a) the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canadians, centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada, and Englishspeaking Canadians, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada;-
My mother, an immigrant to Canada, does not speak fluent French, nor does she speak fluent English. Under this clause, the characteristics of my mother are not fundamental characteristics of Canada. By implication, those who are not English speaking or French speaking do not possess fundamental characteristics of Canada. In my view, this clause is a betrayal of my mother and of the millions of others who have come to Canada from other countries.
The distinct society clause does not adequately recognize the multicultural community in Canada, the eight million or nine million Canadians whose origins are neither French nor English. If the purpose of the first clause in the Constitution of Canada is to articulate what Canada is all about today and what we want Canada to be in the future, then surely a fundamental characteristic of our country today is the multicultural heritage of our communities. However, that characteristic is not present in Clause 1 of the Constitution; nor is the recognition of aboriginal peoples.
Surely when trying to describe what Canada is all about, one would have to recognize the aboriginal peoples as a fundamental characteristic of Canada. Therefore, it seems to me that on the basis of Clause 1 alone, the constitutional Accord cannot be supported.
That clause goes on to say that it is the role of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures to preserve the fundamental characteristic of Canada referred to in the first paragraph. However, it goes on to say that it is the role of the Legislature and Government of Quebec to preserve and promote the distinct identity of Quebec referred to in the distinct society clause. Canadians are asking themselves what that means. Why is Quebec required under the constitutional Accord to preserve and promote the fundamental characteristic, while on the other hand it is a duty of the Government of Canada and the other legislatures to simply preserve it? Is it any wonder that some of those right-wing Premiers from western Canada chose to support this provision? They do not want to promote in any way the fundamental characteristics of Canada, they simply want to accept what exists which is very little and not be required by the Constitution of Canada to do anything more.
My next concern is over the effect this particular Accord will have on the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In my view, the Charter must, and I emphasize, must be supreme.

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
No law from the Parliament of Canada or from any of the legislatures should in any way affect the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. If we truly believe that there are certain rights and freedoms that exist for all Canadians, then surely we must all agree that the Parliament of Canada and the legislatures cannot in any way abrogate those very basic and fundamental rights.
In the last number of months, experts have indicated that the constitutional Accord threatens the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In particular, the women of Canada have made a very persuasive case indicating that the Accord will turn back the clock over that for which the people of Canada fought seven or eight years ago. As a result of this Accord, which was signed in a 10-hour or 15-hour period, those rights for which the women of Canada fought will go out the window. It is possible that sometime in the future the Supreme Court will decide that the distinct society clause, for example, might be used to take away rights for which the women of Canada fought. That ought to be of concern to each and every Member of the House.
My next concern deals with appointments to the Senate of Canada. It is obvious that Senate reform will be impossible as a result of the constitutional Accord because of the amending formula that exists in the Accord. Unanimity will be required to reform the Senate. It does not take a brilliant mind to conclude that Senate reform will be impossible in the future.
Premier Getty indicated at the time the Accord was signed that somehow Alberta and western Canada were winners because of the provision dealing with Senate appointments. All that has happened is that the patronage, if you will, has been transferred from the federal level to the provincial level. A Triple-E Senate will be a dream for centuries to come because of the unanimity requirement in the Accord.
Right now the power to appoint Senators rests with the Parliament of Canada. The Senate of Canada is a national institution. There are safeguards to ensure that Senators reflect the views and aspirations of the different regions. Over a period of time, it seems to me, when we have a Senate completely dominated by provincial appointees, it is obvious their first concern will be for the provinces who appointed them. They will in effect lose track of the national interest.
We have serious concerns over this provision in the Accord. The Liberal Party has called for an elected Senate and I truly believe that if the regions of Canada want equal representation, that is the route to take.
Regarding Supreme Court of Canada appointments, in my view the court is a national institution. The Government of Canada must retain the ultimate authority to make appointments to that court. I ask myself why it was necessary to transfer that authority from the Government of Canada to the provincial Governments. It is obvious the provinces wanted that power because they believed if they had it, over a period
of time provincial appointees would be more concerned with provincial interests rather than the national interest. It seems to me the Supreme Court of a country must reflect the national interest. Therefore the national Government must retain the ultimate authority to make appointments.
Much has been said about the spending power provision in the Accord. I agree with those who argue that that provision is ambiguous. Very little is known about how a future Government or future Supreme Court will choose to define what "reasonable compensation" means; what "program" or "initiative" means; what the word "compatible" or the words "national objectives" mean. I agree with those who argue that in future it may be impossible for the Government of Canada to implement a national program such as daycare when one or more of the provinces might decide to opt out and receive compensation.
As to the amending formula, it is obvious, as I indicated earlier, that Senate reform will be impossible. However, there are other concerns flowing from the unanimity requirement. Others have argued in a very persuasive fashion that the unanimity requirement would make it impossible to create provinces from the Territories in future because one or more of the existing provinces might decide to vote against that and the dilution of whatever authority they might have. I believe that is a serious concern.
I note that you are indicating my time has expired, Mr. Speaker. Let me say in closing that this Accord in my view is not in the best interests of Canadians. It cannot be supported and I do not intend to support it unless the Government in its wisdom decides to adopt the amendments presented by the Liberal Party of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt that the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata) spoke with very strong convictions about his view of Canada. The debate over this matter is one in which the Members will hold different views and hold those views strongly. However, as a westerner, I believe the kind of Canada he proposes in his notion of a different Constitution would serve to rip this nation in half.
He fails to understand the geography of this land, the second largest nation in the world. There are more Members of Parliament from Toronto and Montreal than there are from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, the Yukon, Northwest Territories, and all of British Columbia except for the lower mainland. Two cities have more votes than those people who live on 70 per cent of the land. Yet the Hon. Member says that is just fine. He supports a centralist notion of governing Canada. That concept would work well in England, Belgium or some other geographically small nation like Switzerland, but it defies reality in a country of some four and a half thousand miles from ocean to ocean.
It is a fact that it is our history that makes westerners and Atlantic Canadians and others feel deeply and strongly about
October 8, 1987

regional strength. The Hon. Member should know that when the first four provinces of this country, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario, were formed, they were granted the right to govern their resources. When Prince Edward Island joined one year later it was given the same right. When British Columbia came into Confederation it, too, was given the same right. Yet when the three prairie provinces became part of Canada, they were denied the right to their resources. That was not under their jurisdiction. I remember the old-timers in my province who had fought for 25 years from 1905 to 1930 to obtain the right to their resources. Not in one of those years were they able to raise enough money to pay for provincial needs such as roads, hospitals and schools. The best they ever got was about 30 per cent, this because of a centralist view which believed their resources belonged to Canada.
More recently a Liberal Government put in place the National Energy Program, ignoring the fact that Ontario sold its iron and steel at world prices. It ignored the fact that Quebec and Ontario sold their hydro power at world prices. Every product in every province was able to be sold at world price. However, the Liberal view, and I presume the view of the Hon. Member for York South-Weston, is that a centralist government can impose, irrespective of jurisdictional consideration, a centralist view.
I wanted to make some comments on the Senate but, unfortunately, will not be able to. In conclusion, if we had a Canada such as the Hon. Member proposes we would have no Canada at all because that would tear the map to pieces.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am a westerner. The Member laughs, but British Columbia is the province of my birth. 1 grew up there. 1 understand the problems in western Canada and Atlantic Canada. It is precisely for that reason that we need a strong central government to protect the regions.
The Hon. Member seems to indicate that a strong federal Government is synonymous with Quebec and Ontario, that when we talk about a strong federal Government we are talking about a Government which is more concerned about Quebec and Ontario. That is not the case. The Parliament of Canada exists to represent all 10 provinces and the territories. If the goal is to have equal recognition of the regions, surely we must reform the Senate. With regard to this Chamber we all believe, to a certain degree, in representation by population. Therefore, the Province of Ontario and the Province of Quebec will have, perforce, greater representation in the House of Commons.
That is not to say that a reformed Senate cannot create a better balance in representation in the two Houses of Parliament by giving more equal representation to the regions. That is only possible if we reform the Senate. Under the Meech Lake Accord it will be impossible to reform the Senate because of the unanimity requirement. If we are truly concerned about
Constitution Amendment, 1987
equal representation and, as the Member put it, regional strength, the route to go is to reform the Senate by moving toward an elected Senate in order to give it more power.

Mr. Speaker, the Member and I do not separate on the need for changes in Senate reform. We separate on the Member's notion that the unanimity clause absolutely guarantees that the Senate cannot be reformed. It may make it more challenging but there are examples of very major decisions, including Meech Lake itself, being brought about because of unanimity.
To make the presumption that Canada could never reach a compromised and all-inclusive conclusion among the provinces and the federal Government is to presume that there is a Government of the past in Ottawa which views the provinces as someone to fight against. If you are looking for reconciliation and a federal Government which can work with other Governments, you will see that unanimity is not only possible but has been demonstrated.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that unanimity was achieved with the Meech Lake Accord because the Prime Minister gave everything away. Is it any wonder that the Premiers accepted what was given to them? I do not blame the Premiers for signing the Meech Lake Accord because they received so much in return for so little.
On the subject of Senate reform and unanimity, surely the Hon. Member will agree that the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec alone will never agree to giving Prince Edward Island equal power in the Senate of Canada. Let us not be naive. There is no way a stronger or more populous province will give equal representation in the Senate of Canada to a less populous province. That will never happen. There is more likelihood of reforming the Senate under the present amending formula which requires the agreement of seven provinces and 50 per cent of the population.

Mr. Speaker, many of the people who have spoken in this debate on the Constitution have said that there was bad process involved and that the document itself is flawed. I agree with both of those comments, but must also say that every other time we dealt with constitutional amendments, whether in 1981 or earlier, the process was bad and the resulting document was flawed.
It is ironic that many of the amendments being proposed by Liberal Members of Parliament, many of whom were here in 1981, ask for things for which they did not ask when they formed the Government. For that matter, many of their amendments are counter to the very spirit of what the Liberal Government of 1981 was trying to accomplish.
When I look at the list of amendments presented by the Liberal Party I wonder where those Members were in 1981 when a joint committee studied the document of the then Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau. A number of amendments were moved, some of which were passed and some of which were

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
defeated. These Liberal Members did not move those amendments in 1981, nor did they argue for them. It is somewhat hypocritical for them to say that these amendments are essential in 1987. Having said that, I agree with the content of many of those amendments because they ask for some of the things we were calling for in 1981.
The document with which we are presently dealing is flawed. The Yukon and the Northwest Territories have been hurt by the Meech Lake Accord. It does no good for Conservative Members to say that when the time comes all 10 provinces will be on side. We do not know when that time will come, but we do know that the Yukon and Northwest Territories will have to go through a process which no other province has ever had to go through in the history of our nation. That process will be most difficult.
The provisions which the Liberal Government introduced in 1981 required the consent of the federal Government and seven provinces with 50 per cent of the population before a new province could be created. Now all 10 provinces must agree with the federal Government.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. If Members wish to have conversations I would appreciate if they would go into the lobby or behind the curtains. The Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) has the floor.

The process for the Yukon or one of the territories to become a province will be very difficult. From the history of constitutional changes I know that Premiers, provinces, and the federal Government have their own agenda when they come to First Ministers' Conferences. If a majority of provinces are willing to allow the Yukon in as a new province, it is likely that one, two or perhaps three of the provinces will have other items they want included in the Constitution. Perhaps they will use oil, property rights or another particular cause which genuinely might be important to them as a bargaining chip in supporting the entry of the Yukon. That has been the history of our country in terms of constitutional amendments.
No Prime Minister and no Premier has gained everything they sought. In the future, the Premier of Nova Scotia may have some concerns that she wants addressed in the Constitution and may use the Yukon as a bargaining chip. That is not acceptable.
The other group about which I am concerned with regard to the Constitution is the aboriginal people of Canada. I stated during the special debate on the Meech Lake Accord in June that we have again forgotten the native people of this country. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated that with the Meech Lake Accord, we have completed the circle of Confederation. He was again neglecting the native people of Canada because that circle is not completed as far as they are concerned. There is no process in this Constitution guaranteeing
that their rights will be on the agenda of future First Ministers' meetings. The Government has been unwilling to even guarantee that there will be a meeting in the future to deal with aboriginal rights.
We have asked for this guarantee in questions during Question Period and have suggested amendments to that effect. However, the Prime Minister has not even been concerned enough to write a letter to native leaders or the Premiers indicating that he will put this item on the agenda of a future meeting.
The Prime Minister said in answer to questions in the House that with Quebec as a full-fledged member of the Constitution as a result of Meech Lake we would be in a better position to expand the definition of aboriginal rights in the Constitution to reflect more than the very narrow present definition. The Prime Minister has used that as a reason why we should support the Meech Lake Accord. Yet he will not even guarantee that there will be a meeting on aboriginal issues next year, the year after, or even three years from now.
I consider that to be a failure of the Prime Minister and not of the Premiers, even though the Premiers of British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan were reluctant to move on this important matter of aboriginal rights during the final rounds of negotiations. They are not the ones primarily at fault because it is the federal Government's obligation to represent native people according to the present Constitution and the Indian Act.
The Prime Minister was the chairman of the Meech Lake meetings and should have been representing the native people of this country. The Prime Minister could have at least guaranteed that aboriginal rights would be included on the agenda of the next meeting of First Ministers if they could not have been dealt with at the Meech Lake meeting itself. He should have at least made that effort on behalf of the native people.
My colleague, the Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), reminds me that the joint committee which studied the Constitution during the summer and into the fall recommended that aboriginal rights should be on the agenda, and that it would not breech the spirit of Meech Lake. It would not create any division among the provinces that would result in the elements of the Meech Lake Accord being broken.
The Prime Minister is always willing to go to Washington or attend international conferences. I might say that he speaks with some eloquence on the rights of the oppressed majority in South Africa. Yet he is not even taking a small step on behalf of the native people of this land. He could do so without upsetting the Meech Lake Accord or causing resentment within the population of Quebec. Yet he will not take that step.
I believe his reluctance to do so will hurt him in the next election, because native people have a strong sense of trust in a Prime Minister. They strongly believe in the relationship
October 8, 1987

between the federal Government and native people. When 1 visit the many reserves and other native communities in my riding and talk to native people, especially the elders, they talk of John George Diefenbaker and all the subsequent Prime Ministers as the people who were responsible for making sure that the Government looked after the interests of native people. I am sure the Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) has the same experience when she visits native people in her riding. Native communities have always had much respect for Prime Ministers. They are among the last to become involved in snide politics and personal contests when it comes to the Prime Minister.
When I have occasionally made nasty remarks about one of our Prime Ministers, they have told me they were offended because such remarks are inappropriate.
Native people feel especially grieved by what has happened. They see that the Prime Minister, the chairman of the Meech Lake meeting, is not willing to make any effort to guarantee that the next First Ministers meeting or even the one after will deal with aboriginal issues.

I am concerned about a number of other issues in the Meech Lake Accord. I have said that I will support the Accord because I believe it is important that the people of Quebec become partners in Confederation and share in the process of amending the Constitution in the future. I think it is even more important that they know that there is the willingness, on the part of those of us who are from outside of Quebec, to bring them in, to work with them, to accept the flawed package. I say that because we realize the value of having the mood in Quebec pro-Canada. We recognize the value of that. We are very happy to see that Quebec also agrees that this is an acceptable process.
We are willing, I guess, to swallow some of the things we do not like in the Accord, just as we swallowed things we did not
Constitution Amendment, 1987
like in 1981. It is a flawed document. There are concerns on the part of women's groups, natives, and people in the Territories. There are concerns on the part of people who want to guarantee that the national Government has the ability to act on issues of national concern. But, after having looked at the report of the committee, which represented members from all Parties, I believe that the flaws, and they are there, are not so drastic that we cannot support this constitutional Accord.
We recognize the problems. We have some constructive amendments. We hope that the Government will give due consideration to those amendments. We hope that in the future, when these issues are before the House and when the First Ministers sit down each and every year, we will have a better process, that we do not have the First Ministers, when they have their yearly meeting on the Constitution, sitting until six or seven in the morning and coming up with another amendment to the Constitution, one which the House of Commons has to accept.
It is time that when we deal with the Constitution we have a better process, a process by which people can feel that they are actually in a position to make amendments, in which people who are left out of the process, like the people of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, the aboriginal people of this land, will have a chance not only to have their voices heard but to have a chance to make the type of amendments that are necessary.
My time is up. I want to say that for someone who has been interested in the Constitution for many years, and as someone who took a course, I guess it is over 20 years ago now, on Canada and French Canadians and the history and all the problems that we have had, it is very important, and I am very glad to see that we have a document, although flawed, that does bring Quebec into the family.

I cannot let this moment pass without commenting on my hon. friend's remarks regarding the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the native peoples of this country. As he knows, I was Indian Affairs and Northern Development spokesman for our Party for a year and I became very involved and very interested in the entire scope of problems facing the native peoples. I think what the Prime Minister said in the House should be repeated because to me it made abundant sense. It is fine to schedule meetings. It is fine to say that we will have a meeting next month on it, and another the next month, and so on and so forth. But if nothing is accomplished at those meetings, if they are held just for the television cameras and for everybody to state their positions, they do not achieve anything.
What the Prime Minister said very clearly in his explanation is that the next time they have a meeting-and the sooner the better as far as he is concerned-he wants something accomplished. There is a great deal of work going on now behind the

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
scenes with the native groups and the provinces, who play an integral part in our Constitution, to assure that when we do bring the native situation to the Constitution in a meaningful way that it can be accomplished and that it will be good for everyone involved, especially the native peoples.
The Prime Minister said that there is no sense in calling a meeting just for the sake of having a meeting. We should have successful meetings, and we should accomplish something. That is exactly what is being worked on now, toward that end, for the native peoples of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, what the Conservative Member has said is fine, to a point. We have guaranteed that the subject of fish will be on the agenda at the next First Ministers' meeting. We have guaranteed that the topic of the Senate will be on the agenda of the next First Ministers' meeting. We have no guarantee that we will resolve fishing issues at the next meeting. We have no guarantee that we will resolve the problem of the Senate at the next First Ministers's meeting, unless we bring some big shovels.
So we can bury it.

Yes, so we can bury it. But why not at least have the native issue raised as a guaranteed item at that meeting? Native people will feel there is at least that much commitment. Now they know that they will not be considered at that meeting. It is fine to say that there is work going on behind the scenes, but the Flon. Member also knows that because there is no guarantee of a meeting of the First Ministers on aboriginal rights the funding for native groups has not been increased. For that matter it has been cut. So it is fine to say that there will be meetings of officials but the funding has been cut. It has been made more difficult for native people to prepare their case so that they can get on the agenda of some future meeting. That is the truth.
It is not good enough to say that the Prime Minister has good intentions, that he does want to see it work in the future. He has to do more than that. There has to be some guarantee that that will happen. That is not there, and it is regrettable. But the Prime Minister has not taken the leadership in that area, which is very obvious to the native people in my riding and right across the country.

That is why he is doing it.
The Hon. Member talks about the scheduled meetings ahead. That is right, there are scheduled meetings on certain topics. Those have not been scheduled before in the constitutional conferences. The native people have met three times. I
sat through those meetings and I sat through the native peoples' conferences on the Constitution. The NDP are going around saying the funding has been cut. That is very unfair. The funding ran out on-
It is unfair.

speechtext: It is unfair for the NDP to say it has been cut. What happened is that the program ended and the Government is now looking at a new funding program. It is examining a new way to fund the natives on the constitutional matter. To say it has been cut is untrue. The program ended; that is not cutting the funding.
Will they guarantee to renew it?

Mr. Speaker, I suppose there are many ways of looking at programs being cut or programs ending, but the net effect, expressed in the Hon. Member's own words, is that there is nothing happening at the present time.-

-because the program has ended. It means that native groups are down to a very skeleton staff in terms of trying to develop constitutional positions. It is very hard for them to have meetings in order to discuss these matters with each other. The research cannot be done. Here we are, over six months since the last meeting of the First Ministers on aboriginal rights, and there is still no funding program in place. To say that because there have been three meetings on native issues in the past and they were not successful is not quite true, because they were successful. They brought native issues to national television. There was a population of native people and white people who got to hear for the first time about aboriginal self-government. They got to hear about the problems on the reserves. They got to hear about the concerns of native people. That was a success in itself.
I can tell Hon. Members that in my riding people in native communities were glued to the television sets for each and every one of those meetings because it was so important to them.
It was important for them to hear their national spokesmen speaking articulately to the Prime Minister and to the Premiers. That was very important, and I do not think the Hon. Member argues that point. However, to say that because it has been done three times without success we should not guarantee a fourth meeting at this time is wrong, because it takes away the attention native leaders deserve.
Also, there have been many more than three meetings on the Senate in the House of Commons and in the Senate itself. I think former Prime Minister Trudeau had about 15,000 different proposals on the Senate at which the House looked. We sent committees on the Senate across the land time after

time and, God help us, it is not any better now. It is guaranteed as a topic at the next meeting, and it is certainly not for any lack of attention. It has had too much attention; it does not deserve any. It is a guaranteed topic.
Yes, the aboriginal people have had three attempts, but they are not being guaranteed a fourth attempt because they might be disappointed. I think the native people are willing to risk that disappointment. They want a chance to be heard. They want a chance to be able to negotiate their position. It is being denied them, and that is worse than a disappointment.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary may not have read the concluding chapter of the joint committee report. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was profoundly shaken by the constitutional crisis, and that is why I am delighted to see a peaceful solution to this problem, a solution that respects the values we hold most dear.

I ran for office because I was hoping that I could do directly what I had failed to do indirectly by being involved with citizens' groups. I wanted to find a peaceful solution to the
Constitution Amendment, 1987
problem we had in terms of the aspirations of the Frenchspeaking people of Quebec who wanted to find their place in the sun, their place in the country, and to be able to live as first-class citizens in their own country, speaking their own language and enjoying their own culture. I could not do it through citizens' groups because too many counter-currents were stopping us from really focusing on what was our purpose.
I also felt that the solutions which were being made available through the political process at that time were going to lead to violence. I believe that the use of violence is not acceptable under any circumstance, in any cause whatsoever. Contrary to what some Members of the House might say, that it could be used to help certain causes, I do not believe so.
I think the saddest day for peaceful persons is when they must defend their lives against an aggressor and perhaps kill the aggressor in the process. To me that is a use of violence which is essential but is a very sad one.
Having rejected violence, we had to find an accommodation. Of course accommodations are not as spectacular as the use of violence or the use of aggressive political ways to impose one's vision of the country on other people. However, it would lead to a solution which would be acceptable to me and would be one that would last.
I attended primary school in my native city of Montreal during the 50's. In school, nationalism, our culture and our language all seemed to be wrapped up in the Catholic religion. We were subjected to a type of parochialism which gave us a certain poverty of spirit and a narrow vision of our social, religious and even economic life. I rejected this parochialism because of this vision. In the dictations that we were given to practice our linguistic skills, for instance, we were told that the federal Government was the enemy because it was trying to interfere with our school system, that, because the federal Government was Protestant and Anglosaxon, we might lose both our religion and our language, and that we should therefore not allow the federal Government to interfere with education in Quebec.
This vision robbed us young Quebecers of a modern education system which would have prepared us for the future in a modern country where we had to compete against very sophisticated businesses. By rejecting this parochialism, I also rejected the leadership role which the Catholic church had assumed in the nationalist movement. I therefore had to look elsewhere for a means to achieve my goals, which were to develop as a French-speaking Quebecer, and also as a modern woman in North America who would be able to choose a career either in business, in science or in the arts if I wished, instead of being restricted to certain fields judged appropriate for francophones. In my opinion, the fight of the clergy was

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
too narrow and too focused on their own personal interests. We had to look elsewhere.
By rejecting this parochialism and this narrow vision, I also rejected the vision of the Trudeaus, the Chretiens, the Johnstons, and even, 1 regret to say, the Sheila Finestones. I wanted a country where we could show generosity to all members of our society and to our two cultures. I wanted a wide-open country. I therefore accepted the English fact from a very early date. It might seem strange that I would speak about the English fact because we mostly hear about the French fact. However, for us, in Quebec, the English fact represented the minority. I welcomed this concept with pleasure and I also welcomed the American fact as part of the reality and the vision I had of my own identity as so deeply rooted in my language and culture that it could recognize the beauties of other cultures.
Mr. Speaker, I fear neither the Americans nor the Englishspeaking Canadians. I feel quite confident, but I am always prepared to fight against threats to my language and my culture.
Throughout the 1950s there was something else threatening our language and our culture besides this Jansenism which advocated a much too limited universe for us: economic poverty, or the fact that francophone Quebecers made up most of society's poorer segments. So we had to find a way to fulfill our economic expectations while preserving our language and our culture. With the 1960s came the quiet revolution, and 1 stress the word "quiet" because it was not marked by violence, and the purpose of this quiet revolution was to make us a strong economic people. Then a member of the Lesage government, Mr. Levesque was among those who believed in economic nationalism. Hydro-Quebec was a telling case. I might point out that Mr. Levesque never condoned violence, but he was convinced that we would be able to fulfill our aspirations through the economy. So the quiet revolution yielded an economic lever to remove the obstacle to our development as francophones of French culture in Quebec.
As PQ leader Mr. Levesque also paved much of the road to Meech Lake. Some people are concerned over the weakening of Bill 101 precisely because, in our efforts towards nationalism, both economic and political, because language of work became an issue, that is where we made great progress, but in terms of economic nationalism people also had in mind the question of commercial signs which was part and parcel of the environment in Quebec's society. And today we are concerned that Bill 101 might be weakened because we do not want to lose what we managed to gain during the 1960s and 1970s and the few years after, which is to secure a truly francophone environment in Quebec. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that an honourable solution will be found to protect in Quebec our English-speaking minority, while maintaining the benefits obtained through Bill 101.
The very first explosion of violence occurred in the 1960s. I was still living in Montreal at the time. The first bomb was
placed in front of the U.S. Consulate. At the time, there was a connection with the extreme Left which was very active because of the Americans' involvement in the Vietnam War. There was a leftist infiltration of the nationalist movement which resulted in violence in Quebec. Later on, unfortunately, there was a lot of blood shed by our best young people, because this ideological violence was continued to further nationalism. For us, it was the greatest tragedy. That is when I felt deeply the sadness of living in a violence-prone society: bombs which exploded in residential letterboxes; children who had to remain inside their schools because there was a bomb in a letterbox outside; bombs in department stores or supermarkets. Those were really the darkest pages in our history.
What solution were our politicians suggesting at the time? They were suggesting, it is sad to say, confrontation. They would say: "Let us beat the hell out of these people. Let us smash this nationalistic movement which has gone berserk and become violent", instead of asking why violence had spread among us and was so much a part of our lives.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake Accord is the right way to deal with this pervasive climate that owed its existence to the fact that we let violence and aggressive politics become part of our lives.
As for the economic poverty that prevented us, Frenchspeaking Quebecers, from becoming a modern and prosperous society, the Quiet Revolution changed all that in the 60s. Many of us in the Conservative Party are nationalists who fought during the 50s and the 60s for recognition of the French fact in Canada, and we are now in a party that still believes in economic change that will help francophone Quebecers prosper in this country.
I do not agree with the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte Marie (Mr. Malepart), who gives Mr. Bourassa all the credit because, according to the Hon. Member, he formulated the conditions that lead to the Meech Lake Accord. In fact, the way that was paved by Mr. Levesque was finished by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who worked so hard to bring us to Meech Lake where, if we had not had the negotiating process, Mr. Bourassa's conditions would have made no difference at all. People must communicate, negotiate, and consult. They have to talk about what they want to implement.
All the nationalists who decided to run under the PC flag in 1984 met again in Ottawa, where they have worked in their Party under a leader who had the courage, the vision and the power to gain acceptance for his vision of this country, which is very similar to mine, Mr. Speaker, and to do so calmly and peacefully.
And that is why I am very proud to be part of this Government and to serve under a Leader who has had the courage to go on, despite the many pitfalls. There were times when he was asked to consider specific interests that would have made his ratings rise in the polls, suggestions which he refused to entertain. For instance, he took part in a very fair and very
October 8, 1987

generous debate on the demands of franco-Manitobans. He refused to take the easy way out, to heed the advice of those who told him: Don't get involved, the subject is too controversial, and you will get into all kinds of trouble. Ignore these issues and go on to other things. Just ignore the franco-Manitoban demands. However, he did not take this advice, and he put the experience acquired with the Manitoba question and franco-Manitoban demands to good use when considering the rights of francophones in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, people who accuse the Prime Minister of being lacking in generosity, vision and courage are grossly unfair. I had the same experience as Brian Mulroney who started out with a party that was looked upon as the pariah of Canadian politics because 100 years ago, when Louis Riel was hanged, the Conservatives were in power. Mr. Chapleau told his leader, Sir John Macdonald: If you do that, French Canadians will never vote Conservative again. There was a century of history and tradition to overcome. The Prime Minister, who believed in the economic drive of Canadians, who knew that without a strong economy, a people cannot nurture its language, its religion and its culture, the Prime Minister continued his struggle within the Party.
He could have taken the easy way out and become a Liberal. My riding was Liberal ever since Confederation. The same was true in his riding. He could have decided to become a Liberal like Mr. Trudeau, who left the CCF and the Socialists when he decided the Liberal Party could bring him to power. He changed his stand, but Mr. Mulroney did not. He stayed with the Conservatives, he kept his vision and he led us to the Meech Lake Accord. He has given all of us pages in history which are certainly an improvement over those of the 70s, and he brought to me personally the realization of his dream and the results I had hoped for when I became involved in politics. We found a peaceful solution, a solution respectful of our most cherished values, and I am proud today to speak in this debate which, like the debate on the death penalty, will contribute to our self-actualization.
In conclusion, I would like to tell my Quebec colleagues, and especially my friends such as Don Johnston and Sheila Finestone whom I have known a very long time-I knew him when he was my Member of Parliament in Westmount: Good luck, I respect your ideas, but please remember that we now have a more generous vision of Canada thanks to the Meech Lake Accord.

Constitution Amendment, 1987

Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake Accord provides for the protection and promotion of minority rights in Quebec, but not in the other provinces. Why is the Conservative Party not willing to protect and promote the rights of minorities outside Quebec?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not because the Conservative Party is not ready, but rather because discussions leading to the Meech Lake Accord were aimed at integrating Quebec into the Canadian Constitution. That was the goal of the discussions. At that point, the purpose was not to look at other details and other matters, whose time certainly will come. Among other things, the rights of francophones outside Quebec is a matter of major importance. So are aboriginal rights, the rights of individuals such as the right to own property. There are a lot of things still to be done. The rights of the provinces, the Northern Territories. We still have major matters to look at, but the aim of the negotiations that led to the Meech Lake Accord was to integrate Quebec into the Canadian constitutional family. That was the root of all the violence during the 60s and 70s. So that is what we discussed.
But we did not close the door-to the contrary, the door is now open. If Quebec had not been integrated, we could not have pursued the constitutional process because without the presence of Quebec it was not decent even to sit down and discuss the country, because to me at least the core of the country was absent from those discussions.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the basic features of this country is linguistic duality. But I would like to ask the Hon. Member for Gatineau (Mrs. Mailly) whether she has a definition of the concept of a distinct society. Certainly she must be aware of my interpretation. And I know that many Quebecers have a definition of what a distinct society is all about that is different from mine.
I wonder whether she, as a Quebecer, could give us today her definition in a few words. In order to refresh her memory, I personally will suggest to her that Quebec is different from other provinces because it is the province with a Frenchspeaking majority. But it also has an important Englishspeaking minority and a native component, or anyway a native people that is equally important. That in my view makes it distinctive, that is what Quebec is all about-a Frenchspeaking majority, a very large English-speaking minority and a large native minority. Is her definition different from that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
The distinct society clause in the Meech Lake Accord is quite clear. Its purpose is to enshrine the special character of Quebec and its francophone majority which until now had to be protected by all kinds of legislation because otherwise it could not maintain and enhance its position. As I see it, the Meech Lake Accord is quite clear in that it refers to the francophone majority and the Anglophone minority which is already protected by our institutions and has its own schools, and in fact has a lot more rights than francophone minorities

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
elsewhere in this country. Those are well-known facts, Mr. Speaker. I am not afraid of the terms: "Distinct society", the way some Liberals are, and I fail to see how they restrict the rights of the anglophone minority. In fact, as I said earlier, I am delighted with the diversity of my society. I am delighted by the fact that we are part of North America. I do not feel threatened. I feel strong in the knowledge that I have my own culture and my own language.
I agree that we have a distinct society because we have a francophone majority. We also have an anglophone minority, and we have our native people, who I think are better treated by the provincial government than by the federal Government, for many reasons, because since the provinces each have their own particular problems and priorities, it has been difficult to harmonize the federal policy for our Native Peoples across this country. In Quebec, I think our native people are treated very well.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The time allowed for questions and comments has expired. Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on the Constitution Amendment, 1987.
Mr. Speaker, I come to this debate with a background that has, I think, bestowed on me a very special privilege. First of all, I belong to the franco-Ontarian minority. I was not born franco-Ontarian. I was born in Quebec, and one of my parents was a franco-Ontarian and one was a French-speaking Quebecer.
Mr. Speaker, at a very early age I moved to Ontario with my family, and from then on, we always lived in this province which I call my own. The name Boudria in Quebec goes back to at least 1689, and so I feel my roots are there, although I have no personal memory of having lived there myself.
The question I imagine all Canadians are asking today is, which Members are going to vote for or against the Meech Lake Accord. Before I go any further, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I intend to vote for the Constitution Amendment, 1987. I am not doing so because it is the best agreement that could be made. In fact, I think there are still a number of shortcomings, and I would say major ones. The fact is not whether the agreement is the best possible one. It is not. But the question we ask is this: Is it better to have an agreement or not to have one? I think that as Canadians, we are better off with the Constitution amendment, 1987, imperfect as it is, than without one altogether.
Mr. Speaker, it would be even better if Parliament were to adopt the amendments proposed by my Liberal colleagues. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) and all my Liberal colleagues who took part in the debate in committee and who drafted the amendments.

The amendments our Party is proposing to the 1987 constitutional Accord would make the document better, in my opinion. The amendments would make it better because they would include in the Accord as a fundamental characteristic of Canada the aboriginal people, the multicultural and regional identities and the advantages of developing the Canadian economic union. They would also make the agreement better by offering more protection to official language minorities in Canada outside Quebec. It would also again improve the agreement by ensuring that all provisions of the Charter, not just Section 25 and Section 27, have been included with regard to certain clauses. It would make the agreement better because it better addresses the issue of Senate reform. It would allow for the appointment of Senators from the Territories.
Our amendments would also provide for a deadlock resolution mechanism in the event of disputes. They would ensure greater national consistency in programs available to Canadians. Not least, the Liberal amendments would provide for bilateral agreements between Canada and a potential new province. I am referring of course to the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. My colleagues have also indicated we want an amendment to restore aboriginal rights to the constitutional agenda.
Needless to say, I am of the opinion that these amendments would make the constitutional Accord better. I do not believe any of them are offensive to any of the provincial Governments. We have not heard any provincial Government say they would be offensive. I therefore conclude they would not be. In any event, I ask what would be wrong in proposing these amendments to the provinces?
Unfortunately, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) decided we were not to entertain amendments and therefore I am led to the conclusion that the committee process we went through was certainly not as useful as it could have been. Granted there was some benefit in the fact that we received positive input from a number of Canadians, but it would have been that much better had we been able to fully utilize the information provided to us and which we, the Liberal Party, have used in our proposed amendments.
I want to speak briefly to the unanimity issue. In certain respects I am not quite as frightened of are some people. What we are trying to achieve is a means by which our Constitution can be amended in future. The process cannot be so flexible that one group can have almost free access to changing the Constitution. If that happens it is really not a Constitution, it is just like any other Bill. On the other hand, if it is totally inflexible then it is no longer a living document. We have to try and achieve a balance between the two. That is what makes a good Constitution.
How do we achieve that? The 1982 document with the requirement for agreement by seven of 10 provinces was a
October 8, 1987

good compromise. Etowever, there are perhaps issues on which we would want unanimity. Certainly the admittance of new provinces should not be one of those, in my opinion. That should remain bilateral. Neither am I of the opinion that unanimity is impossible. The fact we have a Meech Lake Accord certainly disproves that theory.
Whether we like it or not, we had a form of unanimity clause even before the constitutional Accord was signed. I say that for the following reason. Only one province did not sign the 1982 Accord. We all recognize that although that province was legally bound by the Accord, there was a certain moral authority missing in our Constitution because Quebec had not signed it. Therefore, we can say in retrospect that, although it was not legally there before, there was still a moral requirement for unanimity. Otherwise, why would we all agree that it was necessary for Quebec to sign the Accord? All the interventions 1 have heard so far, some against and some in favour, have agreed it was necessary to have Quebec sign. Therefore, I conclude that unanimity on that issue was at least a prerequisite to making our country whole again.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, there was a long debate as to whether Quebec was a distinct society, as to what a so-called distinct society was. As a Canadian born in Quebec but who has spent most of his life outside Quebec, I can readily see that it is indeed somewhat different from the other provinces. Whether it is the fact that Quebec's linguistic majority is not the same as the linguistic majority in the rest of Canada, whether it is the fact that Quebec has its own particular legislation, and I am referring specifically to Quebec's Civil Code, whether it is the fact that Quebec has Senate designations-this is peculiar to that province for, as we know, Senators in the rest of Canada represent their province, whereas Quebec Senators represent a specific region-whether it be for a number of other reasons, we all know that Quebec is a society which differs from the rest of the country to a certain extent. Quebec is neither better nor worse for that, but the fact remains that Quebec is a different province. I might single out the fact that traditionally Quebec has had three judges on the Supreme Court of Canada, another element which is certainly distinct or, if you will, peculiar to Quebec as a province.

However, having said that, I think the document would have been improved if we had said that the minority language outside Quebec has an equal status with the minority language inside Quebec. In other words, the document we have now refers to the distinct society of Quebec as having a role of promoting and protecting itself, one of its components being the minority language. The role of this House and the provinces is to protect the minority language and not to promote it. At least the word "promote" is not there. That leads me to believe there is a difference there which is certainly not justified. If that difference in the document were corrected by one of the Liberal amendments, it would take
Constitution Amendment, 1987
nothing away from Quebec but it would make many other Canadians feel much better.

Being a franco-Ontarian I feel that the document might be improved along the lines I have just described without taking anything at all away from francophones in Quebec or from the anglophone majority in that province.
Mr. Speaker, in the past some people said in other speeches that Canada was a country with decentralized powers, and so it is. It has been said that Canada comes second only to Switzerland as far as decentralization of the taxation power is concerned. I find such a statement rather strange since Switzerland is one of the most stable democracies and one of the countries with the highest standard of living in the world, and this comment would seem to suggest that a country which has something in common with Switzerland is deficient in some way. Naturally, this is not be the case, Mr. Speaker.
It is also important to remember the origins of this country. At the Constitutional conferences during the 1860's and even before, at the time of the Union in 1840, the provinces of Upper and Lower Canada joined together under the name of the United Province of Canada. At the time, a majority from both regions was necessary to ensure that the voice of the two components of this United Province would always be heard. We all know that this formula was not practical and it was amended by the British North America Act in 1867.
We must also remember, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is a union of provinces and not a country divided into provinces. Sometimes, my constituents ask me why education comes under provincial jurisdiction. Why did the federal Government give the provinces jurisdiction over education? To such a question, 1 reply: You have the right question, but you are not asking it properly. The fact is that, when the provinces united, they delegated certain powers, including residual powers, naturally, to the federal Government, and kept those which were appropriate for them or which they believed necessary to govern their affairs. Mr. Speaker, the answer to the question 1 asked earlier is this. We cannot change the fact that the provinces have large powers in our system. They had these powers before and they will still have them after the Lake Meech Accord.
What is also important is to emphasize that, without the Meech Lake Accord, repatriation of our Constitution was incomplete, as 1 have already pointed out. As a Canadian, 1 want my country to be complete, I do not want it to be divided as it has been historically on several occasions. I do not want my country to remain under the threat of separation; I want it to be a cohesive and powerful entity. I therefore ask myself this question: Was such a thing possible without the agreement of Quebec, without its joining the Constitution? The answer is no.
A second question which some people ask me is this: Have we paid too much for this agreement? But have we paid too

October 8, 1987
much compared to what? EIow can we make such a comparison? I was not at the bargaining table. The agreement was not negotiated by myself or by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. I am therefore unable to say whether or not something better could have been achieved during the negotiations. I trust that the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition would always be able to negotiate better than the Prime Minister. This is probably true. However, I have to congragulate the Prime Minister for having succeeded in signing this agreement with the Canadian provinces to achieve unanimity and make our country a cohesive and united entity.
Unlike those of many countries, our Constitution is not comprised of only one document. We are sometimes quick to point out that it took us a long time to repatriate our Constitution, from 1931, with the Statute of Westminster, to 1982. However, we should not believe that we have not evolved constitutionally over that time. Our Constitution is made up of 24 documents; 13 Acts of the British Parliament, seven Acts of the Canadian Parliament and four British Orders in Council. The combination of all those documents has gradually amended our Constitution to its present form.
1 hope that that process will not come to an end, that we will continue to evolve and change the document through a slow and gradual process which will ensure that our country is made stronger. Our country will not be made stronger only because more power is given to the central government. It will not necessarily be made weaker because less power is given to the federal Government. Our country will be made stronger if we all work together to keep it the great country that it is. Granted, if we reach a stage where the federal Government has no power and the provinces have it all, that would effectively mean the end of our country. I do not believe that we are doing that with this constitutional Accord.
I would like to speak briefly about Senate reform, something which the Fathers of Confederation probably wanted since the day after the British North America Act was enacted. We have tried to reform the Senate for a long time but have had only very modest success so far. However, that does not mean that the task has ended.
For instance, I do not think it is necessarily wrong that Senators should be nominated by the Premiers. There are those who say that the people nominated by the Premiers will be accountable only to the Premiers. That is not true because Senators are appointed for the rest of their lives. That would be the same as saying that Senators appointed by federal leaders are accountable only to them. We know that that institution has maintained a certain independence in any case.
I know that the time for this debate is drawing to an end. I am happy to have had the opportunity to participate. This is one of the most fundamental issues we will ever discuss. I am of the opinion that the document is not the best one that could
have been signed, but it is certainly better than the status quo. It would be even better with the amendments which our Party has proposed.
