Mr. Speaker, like most Canadians I very enthusiastically welcome Quebec's inclusion in our Constitution which is of primary importance. However, I am shocked and appalled by the Government's failure to provide adequate opportunity for debate and voting on proposed amendments to the Meech Lake Accord. I believe the amendments put forward by Liberals are both sound and vitally important.
These amendments relate to the following: first, the recognition of aboriginal peoples, multicultural and regional identities and the advantages of lower trade barriers between the provinces; second, more protection to official language minorities; third, ensuring that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is paramount and that the basic rights and freedoms of Canadians are not diminished by potential conflicts with any section of the Accord, including equality rights of the sexes; fourth, accelerating the move toward an elected Senate; fifth, that Supreme Court appointments must be made via a mechanism ensuring a full complement of Supreme Court justices at all times and protecting the basic rights of northern Canadians by giving their Governments the same rights as the provinces to propose candidates for the courts; sixth, clarifying the opting out clause where the provinces may opt out of national shared-cost programs, thus ensuring greater national uniformity in programs available; seventh, eliminating the rigid unanimity provision for Senate reform and returning to the seven provinces and 50 per cent of the population formula.
It is absurd that the federal Government will not give these amendments the proper consideration they deserve and take steps to implement them in the Meech Lake Accord.
October 8, 1987

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to seize the opportunity I am given today to draw attention to an important event for the 180,000 people on this continent who proudly bear the Tremblay surname.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, on October 17 and 18 next, more than 2,000 Tremblays will assemble in Charlevoix to celebrate the three hundred and fortieth anniversary of their ancestors' arrival in Nouvelle-France: Pierre Tremblay and Ozanne Achon.
Pierre Tremblay came to Quebec City on August 6, 1647 and settled in 1659 at I'Ange-Gardien where he had four sons. A statue was unveiled in his honour, in 1974, by the mayor of L'Ange-Gardien, Mr. Lionel Tremblay, my father.
Like some other families, the Tremblays came to Canada to settle in the regions of Quebec, Toronto, Vancouver and the Maritimes, and from there populated the rest of the country and part of the United States.
It has been said that more than 20 million people living in Canada and in the United States originate from Quebec and that more than 15 million people living in the United States have Canadian origins.
It would therefore be a good idea, Mr. Speaker, so people could learn about their origin and their roots, to set up information centres that would be better located in the Cities where came the majority of those newcomers, such as Halifax, Quebec City, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
Besides being used as an information instrument, those centres would be an excellent historical and cultural tourism instrument for ethnic groups who came and populated Canada, and from here, the United States.
What do the Tremblays think about that? The matter is open for debate, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: STRATEGY TO FIGHT FAMILY POVERTY URGED
STRATEGY TO FIGHT FAMILY POVERTY URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is National Family Week. While this symbolic recognition is important, it is not enough.
Today's families face tremendous social and financial pressures, and we must provide people who comprise Canadian families with more than one week of recognition a year.
We need a cohesive, comprehensive policy for Canadian families. Instead of inadequate piecemeal programs, we need a strategy for fair taxes for our families, for affordable housing, for accessible child care, for education, training and work opportunities for our young people.
Most important, we need a strategy to fight family poverty. One-fifth of Canada's poor are children. The lack of such a strategy to fight poverty has resulted in food banks becoming one of Canada's fastest growing industries. This is coupled with a disgraceful number of homeless families in Canada.
As an important step I appeal to the Government to announce today that it will drop plans to impose a tax on food. Canadian families have it hard enough without worrying about this possible added burden. I make a special request for those living in the North, where food costs are already between 30 per cent and 50 per cent higher than those in southern Canada.
Northerners in particular, and Canadians in general, do not need and certainly do not deserve a Draconian food tax. Let us help families where it really counts, in the pocketbook.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-ENERGY INDUSTRY BENEFITS
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-ENERGY INDUSTRY BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year Canada exported over $1 billion worth of electricity to the United States. The Americans have unwisely boxed themselves into a corner. Excessive environmental zeal and over-regulation in that country have prevented the necessary construction of new power stations to fill any new demand or even replace aging plants. They will be virtually at our mercy.
The free trade agreement assures the freest possible bilateral trade in energy, and ensures non-discriminatory access to the U.S. market for our electricity. These developments, together with the Minister of Energy's instructions to the National Energy Board to reduce regulation of electricity exports, will ensure a growing and prosperous trade in electricity between the two countries, one which should prove to be very much to Canada's advantage.

subtopic: FUTURE OF FIRESTONE PLANT IN HAMILTON-MINISTER'S ROLE
FUTURE OF FIRESTONE PLANT IN HAMILTON-MINISTER'S ROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the House we saw the spectacle of the Minister responsible for the Firestone situation respond to a set-up question from one of the Hamilton-area Conservatives by saying that he was

October 8, 1987
personally going to involve himself in the dossier of the 1,300 workers who are about to lose their jobs at Firestone. However, when cornered outside the House, the selfsame Minister actually refused to say that he would even pick up the phone to talk to either of the two companies involved. Instead, he promised that he would send a letter-send a letter, Mr. Speaker, when we are in the middle of a national postal dispute.
The Minister knows that 1,300 jobs are involved. How can he stand in the House with the kind of hypocrisy that I have not seen in many years and claim that he is going to fight for workers, jobs, buttress the point made by the other Conservative Member in the House, and then turn around and say he will not pick up the phone, contact the parties involved and get them back to the negotiating table?
If the Minister wants to have a shred of credibility left tell him do not use the mails, get the parties together and save those jobs. Otherwise he has misled the House, he has misled the people and, in particular, he has misled the people of Hamilton.

Mr. Speaker, 1 regret to inform the House, particularly those Members who have served for a considerable period, of the recent passing of former Edmonton East Member of Parliament, Mr. Bill Skoreyko.
Mr. Skoreyko came to this place for the first time in 1958 and, overall, won election seven times, serving the people of Edmonton East for the next 21 years. He was able to do so because of a deep commitment to the people of his riding; a commitment which superseded the pursuit of personal, more prestigious goals. He was, in short, a constituency man who knew how to get things done for his constituents.
I know that I can speak for all Members of the House when, in expressing condolences to Mr. Skoreyko's wife and children, I say that an elected representative can have no finer example to emulate than Bill Skoreyko.

subtopic: CALL FOR AGREEMENT ON BANNING CHEMICAL WEAPONS
CALL FOR AGREEMENT ON BANNING CHEMICAL WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Ottawa is currently host to an International Conference on Implementing a Global Chemical Weapons Convention. The conference is co-sponsored by the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmment and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. The work of this conference is occasion for us in
the House to take note of how important it is to conclude a comprehensive and verifiable ban on chemical weapons production and the destruction of all existing stocks of chemical weapons.
Canada has a particular reason to be as interested in this issue as we are. It was Canadian troops at Ypres who were the first to suffer from the use of chemical weapons in the form of mustard gas.
I urge the Government to spare no effort in doing what it can to secure an agreement on chemical weapons and, in so doing, make a truly historic contribution to international security and disarmament.

maintopic: SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
SUPPORT FOR CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe we have just witnessed the signing of a truly historic free trade agreement, one that history will reveal was a giant step forward for the economic prosperity of Canadians. While the agreement, I believe, was historic, what I hear from the Liberals and the "Old Democratic Party" is hysterical and purely partisan politics, rather than looking at the agreement in the best interests of Canadians.
Let us see what the public is saying about this agreement.
Congratulations on the signature of the free trade agreement. We're really glad now that we have often spoken out publicly in favour of such a pact. We are truly optimistic that 3M Canada's 2,000 employees across the country will benefit from its promise of increased exports and lowered import costs.
On behalf of all these employees and all Canadians from coast to coast we say: great that you pulled it off. And again, congratulations.
John Myser,
President and General Manager 3M Canada Inc.
The telegram says it all. I say to my friends in the Liberal Party and in the "Old Democratic Party": get with it and join with us in moving boldly and with vision into the 21st century.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON NORTHERN ONTARIO
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, people in northern Ontario are very disappointed in the free trade deal which has been signed between Canada and the United States.
In the steel industry we have not gained guaranteed access to the United States market. Even the anti-dumping duties
October 8, 1987

which have been imposed on Algoma Steel are still in place. We are still subject to countervailing duty and dumping duty. There is no dispute handling mechanism in place, only an appeal procedure.
The softwood lumber deal is costing northern Ontario $40 million per year in export tax. It has been enshrined in the agreement, and we are still subject to countervail duties should the Americans decide to impose them.
Most of all, in terms of the uranium mining industry and refining industry, the policy of further upgrading of uranium within Canada before sale to the United States has been abandoned. This policy will return us to being hewers of wood and drawers of water.
I point out to the Government that I think it has made a very bad deal for northern Ontario.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-ATLANTIC COAST FISHERY BENEFITS
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-ATLANTIC COAST FISHERY BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the big winners in a free trade arrangement between Canada and the United States is the Atlantic coast fishery. Enhanced access to the eastern United States market will assure full sales and top prices for Canadian fish and fish products, already a billion dollar industry.
This very year, fish plant workers were demanding government action to remove United States import barriers to restore jobs and employment to Nova Scotians.
Now those barriers will be removed and the fishing industry will benefit, so what does the new guardian angel of East Coast fishermen, Bob White, say? He says that the trade pact will destroy our economy and produce a "dog-eat-dog" society.
Mr. White and the Canadian Auto Workers Union promise to improve the employment conditions of fishermen and plant workers, but they want to destroy and defeat the very initiative which will assure that employment-free trade.
There will be a plethora of disinformation on the Canada-United States trade pact from its opponents, but Bob White better come clean with Nova Scotia fishermen and workers if he wants to retain his credibility as a labour leader. He should leave disinformation about free trade to his friends in the NDP.

maintopic: LABORATORY CENTRE FOR DISEASE CONTROL-OPPOSITION TO RELOCATION
LABORATORY CENTRE FOR DISEASE CONTROL-OPPOSITION TO RELOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express serious concern over today's announcement in Winnipeg that 85 jobs and a major portion of Canada's National Disease Control Research Centre are to be transferred from Ottawa to Winnipeg.
As the Member of Parliament for Ottawa Centre I want to say that there is a great deal of concern among people in my community that closed door decisions to transfer existing federal facilities and jobs to other parts of Canada are not fair. Their basic objection and mine is that this decision was made with no opportunity for public review of the impact on Ottawa, nor of the costs or benefits of this transfer.
I have written to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to express my objections and to ask for such a public process that would end this secret bidding game between communities. 1 am particularly perturbed that this transfer to Winnipeg may substantially increase the operating costs for the Disease Control Centre, because that only can mean reduction in other areas of research at a time of federal spending cut-backs.
It is not good enough just to move a few political plums across the landscape and call that economic development. What we need is a real commitment to jobs in which every Canadian community can be a winner.

Mr. Speaker, I should like personally to congratulate the Quebec Premier, the Hon. Robert Bourassa.
His offer to travel throughout the country to promote the free trade agreement shows that he can rise above partisanship. Mr. Bourassa has said that he is willing to fight within Quebec and outside Quebec to help the passage of the agreement.
After all, Mr. Speaker, we have to choose between a strong and open Canada willing to compete with the other nations of the world during the forthcoming decades, or a Canada which keeps a more traditional, closed and protectionnist approach.
Also the Quebec Premier has chosen the open approach, the one chosen by the Government of Canada. What a difference, Mr. Speaker, with the traditional, protectionist and closed approach formerly taken in Quebec. Well done, Mr. Bourassa!

October 8, 1987
Oral Questions

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON WATER RESOURCES
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after reading the energy section in what actually is an economic union rather than a free trade agreement, I have to conclude with great reluctance that energy in the long term could mean water. Electricity is generated using water. Therefore, it is not inconceivable that 20 or more years from now Canadians could be asked by the United States to ship our water south by way of diversions as the inevitable extension of the continental energy policy the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is committing Canada to through the proposed free trade agreement.
This section looks like the Trojan horse of the agreement, disguising demands for water by the United States in the next century, a possibility that cannot be discounted.
I invite Canadians to let their parliamentarians know their views. The question is this: Is the Government of Canada ultimately committing us, under the disguise of a continental energy policy, to share Canadian waters so as to meet future needs south of the border? If so, is this what Canadians want? And if not, does the Prime Minister of Canada have a mandate to proceed?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-WINNIPEG FREE PRESS SUPPORT
CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-WINNIPEG FREE PRESS SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just returned from Winnipeg late last night. I would like to put a few quotes on the record from an editorial entitled "Free Trade Hysteria" which appeared in yesterday's Winnipeg Free Press. For example:
John Turner's fears for the future are scarcely worth dealing with because they consist of little more than the ritual recital of almost every protectionist cliche ever devised by man.
Mr. Broadbent's argument is more serious, more subtle and every bit as wrong.
The NDP Leader is forced now to concede that all of his fears about Canada agreeing to destroy its social programs, wipe out regional development policies and crush its cultural industries were unfounded. Instead he argues that greater trade with the United States will lead to the erosion of the Canadian view of society that led to development of medicare, old age pensions, et cetera.
The editorial continues:
In fact, all these Canadian social, political, economic and cultural innovations were being developed at the very time when trade with the U.S. and investment from the U.S. were increasing rapidly.
In closing, the editorial states:
The real danger to social programs and cultural industries is not free trade but a stagnant or declining economy. Clinging to the status quo in a dangerously protectionist world would have risked economic stagnation or decline.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister for International Trade. In November 1985, the Prime Minister promised to the provinces that he would not sign a free trade agreement without their approval if it included matters under their jurisdiction. Last night, the United States Secretary of the Treasury, Mr. James Baker, said to some American Senators that there would be no agreement without the approval of the Canadian provinces.
Considering this statement from the Secretary of the Treasury, is the Minister still claiming that she does need the approval of the provinces to go ahead with free trade?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I explained in the House that the Prime Minister has consulted widely with the provinces. He has addressed their concerns in the negotiation of the free trade agreement. He has made it explicitly clear that this is a federal treaty which is within federal jurisdiction, and consent of the provinces is not required.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister is making a very serious and grave error of judgment. The United States Secretary of the Treasury has now declared in front of the American Senate that Americans will not go along with the Accord unless there is full approval of the provinces. The Minister well knows that in the agreement there are a number of areas that touch directly upon matters under provincial jurisdiction, including the licensing of professionals in the service areas, the regulation of the wine industry, the pricing and allocation of supplies of energy, and the list goes on.
The fact is that the agreement does touch the provinces. The Americans have said that they will not sign an agreement without provincial concurrence. Why does the Minister, standing before that evidence, reject that reality? Is it not required that the provinces give unanimous approbation and approval to this agreement if it is to go ahead?
October 8, 1987

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have explained that the provinces have been taken though every element of this agreement. Their concerns have been taken into the negotiations. I see no reason why they would not proceed with an agreement which is in their interests and which they acknowledge is in their interests. I would put the onus on the Hon. Member: deliver us a Premier who will not sign, before he makes those allegations.
Mr. Speaker, when we become the Government, we will be glad to carry out all negotiations with the provinces.
Hear, hear!

Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister. Mr. Dick Self, the chief U.S. negotiator in the area of services, said today in Washington that the Canadian Government had assured the U.S. during negotiations that the provinces would implement the free trade agreement.
A November study done by the Government of Ontario showed that in the area of services alone there would have to be 16 different provincial statutes amended to provide for the kind of access included under this agreement. That clearly means that the provinces have a responsibility, and in effect have a virtual veto right. We want to know when the Government will clearly define and establish the responsibilities and the role of the provinces under this agreement before we go any further down this misbegotten path.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister has indicated what the role of the provinces is, and the provinces have acknowledged that there is the need to be fully consulted and to have their needs taken into account.

subtopic: EFFECT OF AGREEMENT ON HYDRO RATES
EFFECT OF AGREEMENT ON HYDRO RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. In the last few days we learned that Canada lost sovereign control over the price and security of supply of petroleum. Today I want to ask a question pertinent to our loss of control over our hydroelectric resources.
The Minister will know that in the agreement the Government produced there is a clause which says there is agreement to assure the freest possible bilateral trade in energy, including non-discriminatory access for the United States to Canadian energy supplies.
Will the Minister confirm for the House that what this means is that no province will have the right as a matter of policy to charge hydro rates to the citizens or industries of that province lower than the export price to the U.S?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: EFFECT OF AGREEMENT ON HYDRO RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should make it very clear that what we did in the energy negotiations in the free trade agreement was to enshrine our energy policy, not the NEP. The Hon. Member is suggesting we go back and leave the door open to that kind of program.

That condition is inherited from one's family and is most often restricted to a trembling in one's hands.
In about 50 per cent of cases, my doctor tells me, at some stage this transfers to one's voice as well, which happened in my case close to four years ago. It is possible to take medication for the condition, and that is what I have been doing for two years. The medication improves but does not completely solve the voice problem. Speaking more slowly also assists the problem.
This condition is not something which has been easy to accept, even though it is stable and permits me to serve my constituents, I hope well. speechtext: Order, please. Before the House took recess at one o'clock, the Chair had recognized the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper).

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I am glad that I can finally rise to my feet and that we can return to the ordinary business of the House. After the little to and fro that has just occurred, I feel the need to take a large breath of fresh air and relax a bit so that we may focus our attention on the national issues of the day.
The question we are now focused on is that of the Canadian Constitution, the rules by which this country is governed, as well as the Meech Lake Accord and the efforts made by the First Ministers to amend the Constitution. Like most Canadians, I have heard a great deal about the Meech Lake Accord. I have heard many different things about it. It is often confusing when listening to the debate on this question and reading about it in the newspapers because the people that one would consider authoritative have very different views on this matter.
For me, it was important to boil the question down, to try to get at the essence of the matter. For me as a Member of Parliament, it really boils down to whether the Meech Lake Accord is worth supporting, whether or not it has value and whether it is good for Canada. Along with that, I must ask whether the Accord can be improved. Is there any possibility of amending the document? Can the document be further improved? Those are the essential questions for me.
I want to say straight out that I answer in the affirmative to both questions. Is the Meech Lake Accord worth supporting? Yes. Is it possible to improve it? Yes. Of course, I want to elaborate a bit upon how I came to those conclusions and share with other Members, Canadians generally, and my constituents in particular, some of my views on this Accord.
There are a couple of important points which I think need to be dealt with. First is the distinct society clause and second is the spending power clause. The distinct society clause is the gold nugget of this Accord. It has made it possible for the First Ministers of this country to welcome Quebec back into the Canadian family. There are those who have said that from a legal point of view Quebec is a part of the Constitution. It has never been outside the Constitution. In a strict legal sense that
October 8, 1987

is true. Quebec is a part of the Constitution and functions within that framework. The problem is that if you extend that analysis to its logical conclusion, then we do not need to do anything about the fact that Quebec did not sign the 1982 constitutional package. Yet if you do that, you miss the whole point. You look at the Constitution strictly from a legal perspective and forget the question of national identity and whether people feel a part of Canada.
If we are about anything in this Elouse and this country, we are about continuing the process of building a Canadian identity. One unique aspect of that identity is the existence of the Province of Quebec. It gives a special flavour to Canada. One reason we have a level of tolerance for different cultures is because of Quebec. That province, the majority of which is Francophone, has, over the course of Canadian history, had to fight for its rights, its culture, its language. Because the people of Quebec are such a significant part of our country, roughly one-third of our population, although I do not know the exact statistics, they have not only been able to fight on the basis of moral justice but also on the basis of political power.
Let us face the fact that political power makes a difference. If you have political power then you can put into practice your principles and beliefs and bring about good results. It is therefore my fundamental belief that one of the reasons Canada is a mosaic which respects its native peoples and is committed to the preservation of the culture of all ethnic groups is because there is a province called Quebec. The French fact is the reality. Should we ever lose the Province of Quebec then Canada will be that much poorer and we will have a tendency to drift in the direction the U.S. has taken. There is nothing fundamentally wrong with the vision of nationhood carved out in the United States. It is simply not the approach we have taken. It is not the Canadian vision. We have not adopted the melting pot approach. We have formed a cultural mosaic. In large part we can thank the Province of Quebec for that.
What this Accord means to me is that Canadians have opened their arms to Quebec. Canadians have said we want a country tolerant of different cultures and one that respects distinct groups. At the same time I want to say that while I respect cultural differences, while I respect my own heritage as an aboriginal person, while I respect the native groups who live in my riding and throughout Canada, and while I respect the francophone people of this country, that respect does not exist in a vacuum. It comes from the things we share as Canadians. Some may choose to attack the vision of Pierre Trudeau and John Diefenbaker of a one Canada. However, I say that there was an element of truth in what those men said about this country. Their vision has truth in it. Not the entire truth but it has truth. That is why it had the ability to move people. While we respect the cultural differences in this country, and that is important, it is crucial that it be seen in light of the things we share in common. We share a common citizenship. We share a common political structure in which we can live and grow and
Constitution Amendment, 1987
fulfil our potential. A necessary part of that is the capacity to respect the cultural differences which exist among us.
We can say that it is fundamentally important to this country that it has decided to move forward by saying to Quebec: Welcome back to the Canadian family. We want you to be a part of this country. We are willing to stand up and articulate that desire and put it in this country's laws.
Again, when I ask myself the question "Is this Constitutional Accord worth supporting?'' I say yes because it deals with the fundamental nature of this country. It deals with what it means to be a Canadian.
I now want to go to another aspect of the Accord, as I said earlier, which deals with federal spending power. That needs comment because so many people have said that the opting out provision scuttles the capacity of the federal Government to establish national programs. If this Accord had been in place, they say, we could not have had medicare. We could not have pensions. We could not have the fundamental social programs that the Party of which I am a part, the NDP, and before it the CCF, fought for. We could not have those programs which Canadians have adopted not only because they are good but because they express fundamental values that we share as Canadians.
I have taken those criticisms and comments very seriously. I have talked to people who have that point of view and considered what they had to say. When you listen to expert advice from people who have negotiated at the highest levels of government and from constitutional experts who have profound knowledge in this area, you hear a variety of opinions. You must finally make your own judgment, as I have done.
My understanding of the opting-out provision is that if the federal Government wishes to establish a new national program, it will consult with the provinces and if the provinces do not want to buy into the national program, they can opt out and be financially compensated as long as they establish a parallel program. After considering that I have concluded that the opting-out provision does not impair our capacity to govern the country. It does not weaken the central authority or weaken the ability of good, strong political leadership to establish new national programs to meet the needs of Canadians.
This is an area in which I fundamentally disagree with the former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau. There are some aspects of his vision of Canada which I share, one being our common citizenship from coast to coast. However, I think he is wrong in his judgment on the Accord.
I will explain why I believe that the federal spending power is still intact. Before the Accord when the federal Government and the provinces sat down to establish a national program, each party had something in its pocket. The federal Government had federal spending power and the provinces had

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
constitutional jurisdiction. They each had something to bargain with and when they made a deal, we had a national program for all Canadians. It happened that way because Canadians wanted those programs and there was the political leadership to bring it about. There were the Tommy Douglases of this world who wanted to move in that direction.
I do not believe that the Accord has fundamentally changed that situation. When we want to establish new national programs, whether for day care, the environment, the elimination of poverty, or the development of a strong Canadian economy in which all people can work, in addition to its unchanneled spending power, the federal Government will have the capacity to establish national objectives. On the other hand, provinces will have jurisdiction and the ability to opt out if they so choose.
Therefore, we still have two parties with something in their pocket and they will negotiate. If the people want a program and the political leadership exists to establish it, a deal will be made and Canadians will have a new national program. Therefore, let us not say that this Accord scuttles the capacity of political leadership. Political leadership is scuttled by cowardice and a lack of commitment to human need.
This Accord will assist us in addressing the fundamental needs of Canadians. The Accord requires that a strong Prime Minister with a set of objectives and ready to act consults with the provinces in areas of provincial jurisdiction. He would use all of his political muscle, but he would seek co-operation. We will, therefore, create new national programs in a way more sensitive to the regional and local needs of the country. Therefore, I believe that this Accord is worth supporting.
The second question which 1 asked myself about the Meech Lake Accord is whether it can be improved. I have spoken with some conviction about how I see the document. However, I do not want to mislead anyone. This is by no chance a perfect document. We have not arrived at the final objective. The document is not complete. I challenge those who say that we must accept this package without making any changes. There are several specific areas in which this document can be improved. They include the areas of women's rights, the North and aboriginal people.
Not only can the Accord be improved by way of constitutional conferences after it becomes law, it can be improved before. Why wait until it becomes law before improving it? Why not make specific improvements now? The perfect opportunity is fast approaching. A provincial election is soon to take place in the province of New Brunswick. We should take advantage of that occasion to bring to the table items which will improve the constitutional Accord.
I choose the word "improve" because I want to make it clear that I am not speaking of things which would scuttle the Accord. I am not speaking of things which are simply a mask or excuse to try to destroy the Accord. This Accord is valuable and can be made even more valuable.
Eleven political leaders sat in a room together until late at night because they were committed to bring something about. They can do that again. If it means they have to stay there all night, so be it. However, let them improve the Accord so that when we bring Quebec back into the Canadian family other people do not feel left out and resentful, so they do not feel that the only time the political leaders of this country act is when it concerns Quebec while ignoring women, the North, and aboriginal people.
In spite of the value of this Accord it is folly to risk the allegiance of Canadians to this new constitutional arrangement by refusing to improve it. If we can bring Quebec into the Canadian family now we can also bring in aboriginal people, women, and the North.
I believe that fundamentally this Accord is a sound document and that it is good for Canada. We are taking an historic step in nation-building. The step is not complete. If we are not to stumble we must make some changes in the Accord in order to improve it. Let us be clear that we are trying to improve it and not scuttle it.

Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I want to say that I think it is very important the Meech Lake Accord has given Canadians a chance to open the door to Quebec and to French Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, it is important for all Canadians to be part of our Constitution. And today we are very happy that the political leaders of our country are willing to say to Quebec: Welcome to Canada! We are on your side!

I want to congratulate the Hon. Member for his strong speech. There is no doubt that he stated his views with a great deal of conviction for which the House should commend him.
I want to ask him about the so-called generosity with respect to Quebec that he feels lies at the base of this Accord. When we talk about what constitutes Canada, surely he would agree that it is not only because Quebec, a French-speaking province, is part of Canada but that there are French-speaking Canadians throughout the country as there is an English-speaking minority in Quebec.
In my opinion, the Meech Lake Accord does not go far enough in recognizing the fundamental characteristic of Canada because the federal Government and provincial Governments are only willing to preserve this characteristic of Canada rather than promote it.
The Hon. Member is from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He knows that there is a substantial French-speaking minority in his province and his city. I am sure he heard the testimony of the President of la Federation des francophones hors Quebec before the Joint Committee on the Constitution when he said
October 8, 1987

that mere protection is insufficient to prevent or stop the ravages of assimilation.
I would like the Hon. Member to address that particular point. Does he not believe that when we are talking about recognizing this fundamental characteristic of Canada we must go beyond what I consider to be platitudes and undertake to promote this fundamental characteristic?

Mr. Speaker, that is a very important question and I want to give it the attention it deserves.
First of all, as far as the Meech Lake Accord is concerned, I do not think we have finished working on the Constitution in this country. We are about to enter a new stage. I think the Hon. Member is very sincere and has made some very important points, and that it is really up to him to support amendments that will improve the Accord.
Personally, I think it is very important, for instance, for the French fact in Manitoba to be strong and flourishing. 1 remember that when I was a child in Manitoba, when the school inspector came to visit a school, the Catholic students, teachers and sisters had to hide the French books and put English books on their desks. That happened when I was a child in Manitoba, which is not so long ago. However, we have come a long way since that time, and there have been some difficult moments. For instance, we had a very serious debate in Manitoba on how bilingualism in the province should be allowed to develop. A debate that was lost by people like me who were in favour of bilingualism. We were beaten because of a fierce attack by the Conservative Leader at the time, and I can inform the Hon. Member that it is not always easy to progress' as fast as we should wish. And when we can make some progress, I think it is very important for us to do just that.
Perhaps 1 should point out that the Government of Manitoba has just appointed a minister responsible for promoting services in French. I think this is something we can build on for the future. I hope that in the future, we will see greater respect for the French fact in Manitoba. Like the Hon. Member, I am doing what I can in this respect. But quite frankly, this Accord is incomplete where it concerns protecting, promoting or establishing the presence of the French fact outside Quebec.
