Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege, as a Member of Parliament, to be able to speak on a subject of as great importance to our national future as that which is before the House today. The whole question of how we will amend our Constitution is a subject which is at the very heart of our nation.
In commenting on this Accord, I think one must first stress the importance of the effort which has been made to bring about an accord that would seek to accommodate the full participation of the Province of Quebec in the mainstream of the life of our country. I believe all Canadians felt that the country was incomplete without the ability of Quebec to fully participate at the table when constitutional matters were being discussed. There was a great loss to the country as a whole while Quebec remained outside the Canadian community.
Quebec is indeed a distinct community in many ways. It has not only played a unique role in Canada's history, it plays a unique role in the life of Canada today. Therefore, I and I believe all Canadians are pleased that an accord has been struck whereby the Province of Quebec can take its full part in the life of this country.
When we gave approval to the Constitution, it was not possible to have the participation of Quebec because the Premier of Quebec at that time, Rene Levesque, led the separatist party that was in fact seeking to separate Quebec from this country rather than join it. It would have been a

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
total anomaly for that Government to have allowed Quebec to become part of Canadian constitutional life, and the full life of this country. It was therefore not possible at that time for Quebec to become part of the entire process of the country and its constitutional making.
We felt this loss and now, since there is a Government in Quebec that can in fact accept and in fact participate fully on behalf of the people of Quebec in the life of the country, we want to grab that opportunity. We do not know, as we have not known in the past, when a Government might again come into power in Quebec, a Government which might detain or defer that possibility of Quebec having its full role. In fact, it might then be argued by successive Quebec Governments that, "Look, no progress has been made. Canada does not care whether we are part of it or not". They could appeal to the very fact that Quebec was not able to take its full part as an excuse for why Quebec should feel that it had no future in Canada. That is one of the great reasons why I think Canadians are relieved and rejoice that now Quebec and its Government have passed a resolution through its Legislature giving their support to this Accord.
We know that when a proposal was made to the people of Quebec that they should begin to consider separating from Canada, they were appealed to by Mr. Trudeau and by Jean Chretien at that time and asked not to vote in the referendum for the move to separate Quebec from Canada, but rather to vote against such a separation. When Mr. Trudeau and Mr. Chretien implored the people of Quebec, as Quebecers themselves, they said, and promised, that there would be a renewal of federalism. That promise was solemnly made. I think there is now an opportunity for us to show to the people of Quebec that that promise was not made in vain. That promise was made on behalf of those of us who were members of the Liberal caucus at that time. Mr. Trudeau spoke on behalf of our caucus, on behalf of our Party, stating that that effort would be made. So I rejoice with other Canadians that now through this Accord the Province of Quebec can play its full role.
Having said that, and with all my sincerity and all my ability to express how delighted I am about that facet of it, I do think that one has to say that no Constitution is ever perfect. It certainly means, too, that when we start making changes to the Constitution we are dealing with the most fundamental law of the land. It is the most important law. It is the basis of all the rest of the laws of our country. Therefore it is a law which should receive the most careful scrutiny, and the most thorough debate and the greatest opportunity for people throughout the country to make their views known and to express their encouragement of it, or their misgivings.
I also want to say with all the powers at my command, and I only wish that I had the tongue of an orator to persuade my colleagues on the Conservative side of the House that the way that they have approached this matter of looking at and
discussing this very important resolution on the amendment of our Constitution, known by some as the Meech Lake agreement but which also was the Langevin Accord of June 3, 1987, deserves far more attention, far more serious thought, and far more debate than the Government is allowing to the Parliament of Canada, or for that matter to the rest of the people of Canada.
The motion which is before us has not much more importance in the parliamentary procedure than would a Bill put forward by a Private Member. It is appalling to think that a motion is being put before us in the House which affects the very foundation of our country, the Constitution, but that the way in which it is being treated in Parliament is no better, or hardly better at all, than that which can be accorded to a serious Bill that is put forward in Private Members' Hour.
I think Canadians realize that a Bill that has to do with St. Lawrence Seaway funding, a Bill that has to do with the protection of wildlife, or whatever Bill may be put before this House goes through a whole series of complicated processes to ensure that the democratic process takes place. With almost all Bills in the House of Commons there is first a debate in principle. That debate can go on and, usually, unless some kind of time allocation is brought in, every Member of the House has a chance to talk about it in principle. Then it normally goes to a committee. It goes either to a standing committee or to a legislative committee where the Bill is looked at, discussed and talked through. Amendments are proposed at committee. Then, having had a vote first of all in the House on principle, having been before the committee, it comes back to the House for another debate. There, in that debate, is an opportunity in the House itself, to put forward amendments and for each one to be considered and voted upon. Then, after those votes are over and that stage is passed then still another debate is held. In that third stage there is still an opportunity for more discussion and further thought before a final vote is taken and the Bill is passed.
I think that shows that in our democratic process we want to make very sure that in Parliament anything we decide has been given deep and due consideration, in fairness to all concerned. It shows that we have given an opportunity to the people of Canada to make their positions known through the committees, to give them an opportunity, in time, to write to their Members or communicate with their Members as to their views so we do not make any mistakes.
That is what happens with any normal Bill, a Bill that deals with perhaps some of the less important matters of the country in the House, at least less important than we would say is the Constitution of Canada. Yet the Constitution of Canada is being amended. It is being put before us with a time span and a way to deal with it far, far less democratic and far less thoughtful than would even an ordinary Bill in this House of Commons receive, or a Private Member's Bill for that matter.
We have placed before us one total package. We are able to give one kind of amendment, as a Party, to this Bill. In short,
October 8, 1987

we have but one debate on it. It went of course, to a committee over the summer, and then one debate. Then, when it is passed that is it. That is what the House of Commons can do with the Constitution of Canada, with the amendment of the most fundamental law of all, the Constitution of this country. It is amazing. It is bewildering that this is the only way in which we can proceed.
I think that if we look back at how the constitutional debate was carried on in the past, we would realize that a great deal of thought and a great deal of time was given to that debate- months and months and months. There were discussions among the provinces. The matter was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada for its opinion, to test out whether what we were doing was the right way to proceed. The views of the Supreme Court were taken into account, and changes were made.
I would like to point out further that when people or groups came to Ottawa, or sent their views to Ottawa about changing that constitutional Accord, their voices were finally heard. We saw that when the voices were lifted on behalf of the women of this country, in terms of their misgivings about the language or what was being taken out or what was in the Constitution, their views were listened to, perforce. That is the way it should be.
Changes were made again, with the provincial Ministers giving consideration to those proposals. Meetings were held, bringing them back again to see if further changes could be made. I remember very well the indignation of members of the Conservative Party who were in opposition at that time at the thought that they were not being given enough time to discuss such an important issue as the Constitution of Canada. Day after day they rose in their places and extolled the virtues of democracy, the importance of openness in Government, the importance of full participation, and the importance of opportunity to debate. I think many of us listened to their concerns with some sympathy.
In this particular debate we find amendments being made to the Meech Lake agreement which in fact might greatly hobble future changes in the Constitution.
It is true that the Constitution is and will evolve. However, because of the Meech Lake agreement or Langevin agreement in some cases the Government of Canada has made such evolution practically impossible in that the formula for amendments requires unanimity. It can be said that sometimes it is possible to obtain unanimity from the provinces. When we consider the fact that it will be possible for a province, because of someone like we had in Quebec, to prevent the approbation of what is reasonable and good for the country, to stand in the way interminably of progress which may be needed immediately in terms of changes to the Constitution as a result of some unforeseen problems.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
This is why we in the Liberal Party feel that the Government should be open and should be listening not only to us as a Party but to the people of Canada who also have grave misgivings about this formula and about other matters. This is why the Liberal caucus has come forward, through the motion of our Leader and through the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), to indicate that the Meech Lake Accord should be amended to deal with some serious matters.
In my view one of the most serious matters concerns a return to a formula whereby we have seven provinces and 50 per cent of the population voting for an amendment to the Constitution rather than total unanimity of the provinces as the Meech Lake document suggests.
Time after time the Tory Government has proven its unfortunate proclivity to talk in very fine and glowing terms about democracy and about parliamentary reform. However, on the most important issue upon which we could possibly be focusing, it provides for us and for Canadians little opportunity to give proper thought to and debate on these matters. We cannot move each amendment one at a time as we should be able to do. We should be able to look at it, discuss it, and honestly reflect upon it because it is so important.
Since the Government has a tremendous majority in the House of Commons, I do not deny its right in the end, after debate, to decide that there will be no amendments. I would not deny that the Government has that right, but it should not deny us the right to make amendments and to have each one of them carefully considered by the House and by the people of Canada. We should be able to go through first, second, and third readings, to vote on each section, to look at the amendments carefully, and to give the most important law of the country clause by clause consideration.
There is not enough time for me to deal with all the amendments which have been put forward by my Party as very positive suggestions. Large segments of our population, such as women, who represent over 50 per cent of the population, aboriginal peoples, multicultural people, and those concerned about the future of the territories, have expressed misgivings about the present text of the Accord. They wish it to be improved or amended so that there will be no doubt about the matters which concern them. While I cannot deal with each of the amendments we have proposed to deal with the concerns expressed by these people, I call the attention of the House to some of them.
One concerns the future of the Senate, which I believe would be strengthened and made more meaningful if it were an elected Senate. Clearly this is the position of our Party.
Rather than continuing with a formula which entrenches the future of the Senate as an appointed body and provides a situation wherein the provinces may feel that they have some kind of investment in keeping the formula as it is in the Meech Lake Accord, let there be freedom, let there be breath, let there be life; let us breathe a new life into the Senate rather than stultify it along the lines of the Meech Lake Accord. Let

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
there be a move at this time to have future Members of the Senate elected. Then the process can be worked out in further conferences between the provinces and the federal Government. Further consideration could be given by the Elouse and the Senate so that the Senate would play an even more dynamic and more important role than it does now.
Another of my concerns is in the area dealing with equality of the sexes, the rights of men and women being guaranteed and protected. We want to ensure that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is paramount, and that the basic rights and freedoms of Canadians are not diminished by potential conflicts with any sections of the Accord, including sexual equality rights.
It would be wise if the Conservative Government would wake up to the realities which exist. There has been an example of this before. When the women of the country expressed concern, the Government of Canada under the last administration paid attention by making changes to the Constitution which took into account the solemn and sincere concerns expressed by them. Why does the Government minimize the importance of the concern expressed by women and their representatives, as well as by men concerned about the rights of women? They wonder whether the Meech Lake Accord perhaps puts into jeopardy the rights which were presumably obtained in the last go-around on the Constitution.
Those are some of the matters I wanted to bring to the attention of the Government. I ask it to consider them as being not only the views of my Party but the concerns expressed by the people of Canada. Will it not listen? Will it not open its ears to the concerns of Canadians who are happy to see Quebec being involved and being brought into the full life of the country?
They do not want to be accused of being unhappy about this, ungrateful or lacking a sense of patriotism because they want to bring up matters and points which they feel are very important for the future life of Canada, points which concern them and therefore life in this country as well. It is not an act of treason. It is not an act of lack of patriotism to be concerned about other issues in this Accord. Just because one expresses a concern about it, that does not mean one is not happy about the fact that Quebec is now brought into the full life of Canada.
Let us try and, in a spirit of understanding, move toward the possibility that the Government may still consider going to the provinces in the light of these proposed amendments which we have made with full sincerity and let them respond to the people of Canada and, in the same spirit, discuss with the provinces the way in which we can amend this Accord without trashing the Accord in its entirety. I do not think we need to throw out the baby with the bath water. I think we can try to amend, improve and repair what could be a much more perfect document so that future generations will say that we gave
them something which they could change in the light of their future, that we did not deliver something that was a fait accompli which closed out any future evolution of the Canadian Constitution.

Mr. Speaker, the Member for Eglinton- Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) was in this House in 1981 when we voted on the patriation of the Constitution which included a Charter of Rights. That Charter of Rights in Articles XVI to XXIII provided citizens with services in the official language of their choice. It dealt with minority language education rights. What we did in 1981 was to put in the Constitution in some respects the official languages policy which had prevailed for a period of 10 or 12 years prior to 1981.
As I understand it, those policies were based on the principle of linguistic equality, namely, that we were trying to achieve an equal status for the English and French languages for persons who speak English and French as much as possible throughout the country. In my opinion, the Meech Lake agreement goes against this principle of language equality because rather than having the same rights in Quebec as we have in Ontario or British Columbia, the possibility arises that rights may be different in one part of the country to the other.
Does the Member not agree with my interpretation that we are really retreating from the principle of linguistic equality with the Meech Lake agreement?

Mr. Speaker, I believe the subject which my colleague has brought forward is most important. The fact that he is concerned about it, as all Canadians should be, is clear that we are putting into language in the Meech Lake Accord matters of concern to people regarding their right and their children's right to be able to function fully in one of the two official languages of their choice and thus function fully throughout all of Canada.
I believe the intention on the part of those who signed the Accord was to achieve that. The question is, have they? That, first, is a matter which involves a great deal of legal expertise and interpretation. I am not going to propose that I have that constitutional expertise to give a wise opinion on the matter. If there is some doubt, it would not be a bad idea for us to incorporate in the language of the Accord that kind of reassurance. I have been pleading with my Government colleagues in this House for the Accord be made that much clearer so that people who have anxieties about it, not just for themselves but for the country and future generations, can understand it. We could then have legal experts conclude that yes, this is what it says. Unfortunately, we heard a wide variety of opinions in the committee. Therefore, that gave us reason to look at the proposed amendments made by our Party. We should talk about them, not just have concerns. We should be promoting the protection of languages in the provinces. Governments have a responsibility to promote and protect them as well as to acknowledge their existence.

October 8, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I have a brief comment which will be followed by a question to the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille)
My colleague mentioned his support for an elected Senate. I recall reading a statistic which pointed out that something like 99 per cent of all Canadians would never run for elected office. If that is true, one would have to question whether, in fact, not only federally but provincially, the country is being well governed.
In that sense I have always felt the Senate does have a good role to play. Very talented, experienced and dedicated Canadians have a chance to serve their country by being appointed to that august body. Would the Hon. Member give me his views? An appointed Senate could be devoid of partisanship but it would not if we had an elected Senate.

Mr. Speaker, there may be some people in this august Chamber who are looking for an appointment to that other place. 1 do not want to be facetious, but I had to make that remark. There are probably a fair number of people who might look at that other place as being a good place to which to be appointed.
When my colleague said that 99 per cent of the people of Canada would not run for office, while they may not want to in the sense that it might be difficult because of leaving families-which many of us have to do to come to Ottawa or to go to some other place if one were a provincial Member- when the time comes and people are approached by fellow citizens and asked to run for office, even though they may have said no, that they would never run, they do respond. This reluctance to serve occurs with jury duty. I do not think anyone pounds on doors to get on a jury panel. But people serve because they feel it is genuinely important to make that contribution for their country.
As for the other small point, 1 do not have the time to enter into a debate about an elected as against an appointed Senate. I have expressed my views, and I think it is an important point. In general, the people of Canada feel that it would be a good thing if a chamber with such powers as the Senate presently has were also elected. They would then know that these people are there because they were elected by the people of Canada and not because they were appointed into a political position.

If I were to give my remarks a title, Mr. Speaker, I would call it the legitimacy of the Constitution. First of all, I should like to set the constitutional Accord in its proper context by saying that, together with a great many Quebecers, including Mrs. Chaput-Rolland who appeared before the Parliamentary Committee, I felt deeply hurt when in 1982 the Constitution was patriated without Quebec's consent.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
1 was certainly for the patriation of the Constitution combined with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. But I deeply regretted and even objected to the fact that these political decisions were forced upon Quebec; as much as I objected to the decision of the Imperial Parliament in 1840 to impose the Union Act and to ban the use of the French language.
Although, as Hon. Jack Pickersgill reminded the Committee, the Parliament of Canada with its English-speaking majority insisted in 1867 on re-establishing the linguistic rights of French-speaking Canadians, the latter will always remember the attempt made in 1840 at depriving them of their rights and they are looking for assurances that such an experience will never happen again. Together with a great many others, I feel that it did happen again in 1982. Once again, Quebec was ignored.
In a speech he made on April 15 of this year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) clearly indicated what was at stake at the Meech Lake meeting, and I quote:
"With the Constitutional Act of 1982, we have now a fundamental law governing our country, a social contract which is binding upon Quebec without the consent of its National Assembly.
It is unacceptable that recent wounds have not yet healed. Quebec, as a distinct society which enhances Canada, has to join the constitutional family.
For that purpose, we have to find a fair balance between the concept of equality among all provinces and the need to protect and strengthen the unique character which Quebec gives to Canada.
The isolation of Quebec was a problem we had to assume when we came to power. We cannot bequeath it to another generation which would perhaps have to resolve it under more difficult circumstances and in less propitious times.
The Prime Minister knew that the problem had to be solved quickly. He knew that the country, that Quebec could not go on living with a constitution which had not been accepted by all the partners in Confederation. He knew more particularly that values could not be imposed to a community and that a document as important as the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to gain its true worth had to be freely accepted by Quebec. This Charter of Rights and Freedoms represents common values shared by the people, it is a definition of its collective will. The real strength of a charter is based on the intensity of feelings for it shared by the citizens.
Therefore, as long as Quebec will not freely adhere to the Canadian Charter, it will remain weakened.
The Parti Quebecois Government was ready to negotiate a constitutional agreement in May, 1985, provided that the greater part of the Charter did not apply to Quebec. It was an unacceptable condition for those who believe that Canadians can share the same ideals of justice and equality.

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Finally, a federalist Government in power in Quebec since 1985 is getting ready to adhere to the Charter of its own free will and to acknowledge its legitimacy.
And now Canada, through its First Ministers, says it is ready to welcome Quebec under conditions that are good for Quebec and for Canada. Parliamentarians and citizens across the land are asked to join together for that purpose.
I am pleased with the consensus of the three leaders- including our Liberal colleagues-who view Quebec's return to the great constitutional family as a significant national goal. This clearly shows that the First Ministers' appeal has been heard by our parliamentarians.
The Parliament Committee has also shown that the appeal was equally heard by politicians, former civil servants and well-known English-speaking academics. The Committee Report suggests that nearly all the witnesses who appeared at the hearings unanimously recognized the importance for Quebec to resume its place of its own accord within the Canadian constitutional family. Those Canadians who appeared before the committee also insisted that it was most important to solve the dispute between Quebec and the rest of the country; the Accord struck a remarkable balance between Quebec's own interests, the principle of equality between provinces and the national interest; the Accord in no way infringed upon the rights of Canadians, and this opportunity should be taken to adopt the resolution that will open the second round.
That was the view voiced by Gordon Robertson, who was Cabinet Secretary from 1963 to 1975 and Cabinet Secretary on Federal-Provincial Relations from 1975 to 1979-he is one of the most experienced negotiators on constitutional affairs in Canada.
That also was the view of Robert Stanfield, who led our fellow-citizens in Nova Scotia before coming over to the federal scene.
This is also the opinion of Peter Meekison, former Deputy Minister of Federal and Intergovernmental Affairs of Alberta.
Moreover, it is the opinion of the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, who served with distinction under four Prime Ministers of Canada as a Minister and as a public servant.
It is also the view of Professor William Lederman, one of our most eminent constitutional law professors. It is the opinion of Peter Leslie, Richard Simeon and others, who have a very open minded and sensitive attitude toward Quebec.
I have every confidence that the appeal of the Premiers, who have the support of Quebecers and of many Canadians, will be heard by the Parliamentarians. Moreover, by repairing past mistakes, the 1987 Constitutional Accord will open the door to a new era in Canada by recognizing a fundamental characteristic of our federation.
By entrenching linguistic rights in the Constitution in 1982, we legislated to put behind us once and for all past attempts,
such as in the Union Act of 1840, to make French disappear from Canada.
With the 1987 Constitutional amendment, all Canadians are giving their enthusiastic support to the concept of linguistic duality as a basic characteristic of Canada, the role of all legislative assemblies and of Parliament to protect this characteristic is being confirmed and the distinct society of Quebec joins the Canadian family.
Finally, our linguistic rights find new grounds for existence in our Constitution, Canada finds its soul and Canadians rejoice in their diverse character.
I believe that we cannot be indifferent to the fact that the Constitution was imposed on Quebecers, that they rejected its legitimacy and that Canadians do not at this time share freely accepted common values. The First Ministers did not remain indifferent to these facts this year, and neither did the distinguished Canadians I mentioned earlier.
A country is more than a series of abstract and rational concepts. To develop, it needs a soul. I believe that by voluntarily joining the Constitution and the Charter of Rights, Quebec is giving back this soul to Quebecers and Canadians. Quebec is finally telling Canada that it is willing to share in the dreams and aspirations of our great country and that it also shares its values in its own way.
This is why I believe that the signing of the Meech Lake Accord was an event of great moment for Canada and why I ask the House not to make it necessary for us to go back on this Accord.
In conclusion, I would recall the words of the committee and urge people who refuse to listen to the First Ministers' appeal to reconsider their position. To them the committee is saying:
If one is to maintain that the terms of the 1987 Contitutional Accord should not be accepted because they exact too high a price in terms of their vision of Canada, then one must be prepared to accept that at least in the foreseeable future Quebec will remain officially estranged from the Constitution and that a Constitution without Quebec will continue to limp along without the willing participation of one of the key parties to Confederation.
That is the kind of future the opponents of the Accord envision for Canada. That is what most Canadians want to avoid by supporting the Constitutional Accord of 1987.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak in support of the agreement commonly known as the Meech Lake Accord. I want to point out some very serious concerns which I think many of our colleagues have been expressing.
It seems to me that Constitutions of countries are very much like those of organizations which reflect the basic beliefs of, and establish over-all objectives as well as legal requirements for, its Members. They are rarely perfect but must be tested against experience and continuously adapted to reflect the
October 8, 1987

concerns of the entire organization as well as its component parts. Therefore, in a country as complex as Canada we must entrench national concerns and obligations as well as our historic concerns while responding to the very diverse needs of different regions and ensuring through our Charter of Rights that the rights of all our citizens are adequately protected.
It is interesting and significant to note that the Canadian Constitution is only about five years old. A very immature Constitution it is. I am sure all of us who have gained from this current review and analysis-those who were on the committee, of course, are now experts-would agree that there are very serious flaws, particularly in the Charter, which must be redressed. Some Members have felt that it is perhaps flaws in the Charter rather than flaws in the Accord which need further attention.
There are amendments that we want to see to the Accord itself. We all agree that the overriding flaw in the 1982 agreement was the fact that Quebec was not part of the Constitution of Canada. That was the primary objective of this round of negotiations toward constitutional review and amendment provided that it did not diminish any other rights.
This Accord brings Quebec to full and active participation in the patriated Constitution for the first time. We in the NDP are very pleased that this is the case. In our view it acknowledges that Quebec is a distinct linguistic and cultural society within Canada. It reflects resolutions which the NDP adopted as a priority at our 1987 convention in Montreal. We acknowledge, however, that there are a number of flaws in the Accord and we strongly urge the Government and the First Ministers to correct those flaws before it is passed into law.
It is important to recall that the process involved in this round of constitutional reform leaves very much to be desired. In my view it did not reflect the democratic process. We should remember that in the decisions made behind closed doors at Meech Lake there were no natives, northerners, women or the disabled represented. These decisions were made by 11 men, all white, who drafted a Constitutional Accord to be applied to all of us in Canada. There is no question that they did a remarkable job as far as they went, but after further study and consideration, particularly by the groups I just referred to, there are indications that serious flaws exist. We believe those flaws can be corrected with three simple amendments without jeopardizing the Accord itself.
I want to concentrate my remarks on two areas of particular concern, but before doing that I would like to quickly review the amendments we have put forward and which were expressed in a letter from our Leader to the First Ministers.
There are three essential amendments and they are consistent with the objectives of the 1987 Constitutional Accord. Our first amendment concerns fairness for Canada's northern citizens. We believe First Ministers should immediately remove the anomaly of Canadians living in the territories being denied the opportunity available to other Canadians of serving on the Supreme Court of Canada and possibly in the
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Senate as well. Of course, we as a Party are not as concerned about the Senate. As well, First Ministers should address the injustice of requiring unanimous provincial approval for the creation of new provinces, a degree of concurrence not required for any of the existing provinces.
Second, we believe the Accord should include a commitment to hold a First Ministers' conference to discuss aboriginal rights, in particular self-government. It should be amended to ensure that representatives of aboriginal peoples and the territorial Governments can participate fully in these discussions.
Third, we do not believe the linguistic duality-distinct society interpretative clause abrogates, supersedes or overrides sexual equality rights, or any other rights guaranteed in the Charter. This is the conclusion which our representatives on the committee came to after very thoughtful analysis of the expert testimony. However, there is doubt across the country and therefore we say the same abundance of caution reflected in Section 16 when it was added can be applied to sexual equality rights without jeopardizing the Accord. Therefore, we urge First Ministers to amend the Accord by adding Section 28 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which, as we all know, would reaffirm the equality of men and women.
We also recommend a complete Charter review, particularly regarding minorities, including visible minorities and disabled persons, in the very immediate future. We should give greater consideration to recognizing ethnocultural realities. We do not agree with the process that took place and we are very strongly recommending that any future process must be much more democratic with an opportunity for public input. This should be done through a standing committee of the House of Commons.
I want to concentrate my remarks on two areas of concern, particularly from the point of view of social policy. Those two areas deal with federal spending powers and the protection of equality rights. Both areas have been raised as concerns by social policy advocates and many women's organizations. In fact, women's organizations continue to raise these issues.
As to spending power, the Accord specifies that provinces will have the right to opt out of national programs but may still have costs shared by the federal Government provided the programs are compatible with national objectives. I must confess that as a strong advocate of federal leadership in social programs and with a very major concern about a national child care program, I was very concerned about this question.
Would it weaken the impetus for a national child care program which is urgently needed in Canada? Would it have prevented medicare from being established as a national program with enforcement of the five national principles which are implicit in medicare? Would it allow provinces to do what they wish with federal dollars as they have in the past with

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
federal moneys which have been transferred for post-secondary education?
There is no more urgent need in Canada today than the need for a comprehensive national child care program which will ensure the availability of a range of quality, affordable, flexible child care services in both rural and urban communities. The child care situation is a crisis. This has been documented repeatedly.
A national child care program was promised in very strong terms by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), but it is obvious that no action is being taken on this. I cannot help but wonder whether the delays are in any way related to the process of this Accord. Under the new Accord the federal Government has the right, in our view, to establish a national program of child care with clearly defined objectives which must be the criteria for provinces if they are to receive federal funding for child care.
The Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association, the National Anti-Poverty Group and others spoke strongly of the need for the Government to establish right now these national objectives and to outline the requirements for any national child care program which will receive federal funding. These organizations expressed fear that there would not be clear objectives established.
I share these fears, but I have concluded, as have my colleagues, that these fears are not related to the Accord so much as to what the Conservative Government will or will not do with regard to child care. We see it as a very important political issue. The Accord definitely obligates the Government to state national objectives which reflect its philosophy and will establish clear principles for provincial programs which receive federal funding.
We conclude that the problem is political rather than constitutional. A New Democratic Government will make child care a top priority and will establish clear, progressive objectives as a requirement for any provincial programs which enter into cost-sharing arrangements.
Medicare was started as a provincial program by Tommy Douglas in Saskatchewan and became a national program. We strongly agree with the revisions to the health Act which were brought in by the past Minister, Monique Begin, which enforced the five principles of medicare with penalties. Such provisions should be included in all programs which receive federal funding. We are convinced that this kind of federal authority over spending powers remains under the new Accord. In fact, experts believe that the Accord strengthens the use of federal moneys provided that the federal Government defines these national objectives.
A national child care program will be the test of this section of the Accord. It will be the test of the Government as well. I have repeatedly asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to establish national child care objectives
which will designate quality, affordable, accessible child care services as a base for any federal financing arrangements.
Finally I come to the aspect of the Accord which continues to be a very major concern to women's organizations across Canada. This concern, rather than diminishing, is escalating. We cannot ignore it. I implore all Members of the House, the Government, and First Ministers to give it major consideration. After major analysis, including analysis by legal experts, women's organizations still have a fear that sexual equality rights may be at risk under the new Accord.
1 do not want to refer again to the many presentations which were made to the committee. I would like to pay tribute to my colleague, the Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), who contributed a tremendous amount of energy and expertise to that committee and our caucus. There is no one more concerned about equality rights for women as her history and record show.
I think I reflect her opinion when I say that we may not have the same concern about this as far as the Accord is concerned. However, we do agree that the concerns of women across the country must be dealt with. They must have the opportunity to express their concerns and have them reviewed as they have been requesting.
In summary, I would like to refer to two very recent letters which implore the Government of Canada and the First Ministers to consider their appeals. The first letter is an open letter of October 4 to Members of Parliament from the Ad Hoc Committee of Women on the Constitution. I will read an excerpt from that letter. They state:
-governments want women to accept their assurances that the Accord's risks to gender equality are minimal; women are adamant that any risk is unacceptable, no matter how small.
Accordingly, they ask us to support recommendations made by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women on September 23. The letter continues:
Specifically we seek your support for:
funding through the federal Secretary of State for a women's national constitutional conference.
It is hoped that this conference would find a way to amend the Constitution without re-opening the discussions on the Meech Lake Accord in a way which endangers Quebec's recognition in the Constitution.
No women, and I am sure no Canadians, want to jeopardize that aspect of the Accord.
They further state:
-that an urgent federal reference to the Supreme Court of Canada on whether the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms is detrimentally affected by the Meech Lake Accord-
-be undertaken.
The federal government must undertake to consult the CACSW on the question and should guarantee that the CACSW-
attends at the hearing.
Subsequent to that we today received, as I imagine other Members have, a very urgent letter from the National
October 8, 1987

Association of Women and the Law dated October 6. This is a very reputable group comprised of outstanding women lawyers who have expertise in constitutional matters. The letter reads in part as follows:
We urge you to consider our concerns. In our brief submitted to the Special Joint Committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on the 1987 Constitution Accord on August 4th, 1987, we raised a number of concerns relating to the status of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and in particular women's equality rights.
We continue to be concerned that by enumerating some rights in Section 16 and in specifically mentioning the Charter in other sections, the courts may interpret this as excluding or giving less scrutiny to other rights, including women's equality rights. This may create a hierarchy of rights.
In addition, the Supreme Court of Canada decision concerning Ontario's Bill 30, pronounced on June 25th, 1987, would seem to create a hierarchy of constitutional documents, by making some sections of the 1867 Constitution Act immune from Charter review. The Department of Justice has used these arguments in the challenge from the Yukon Territories.
In order to ensure that this is not the effect of this set of constitutional amendments, we believe that the Accord must be amended to clarify the relationship of the Charter to these clauses, in particular to the new s.2 of the 1867 Constitution Act dealing with language duality and Quebec as a distinct society.
It is important to note for the record that they advocate a women's national constitutional conference with the objective of developing an amendment to the Accord which would not endanger the Accord or Quebec's recognition in the Constitution but would protect charter equality rights. Our Party strongly believes that this would be helpful. We advocated the inclusion of Section 28, but we would certainly support an improvement on that.
They also ask that the resolution in the House be deferred until this convention can take place. That might be very difficult. They go on to say: "We ask you to support a Reference to the Supreme Court of Canada from the federal Government. In this way, we can all receive a judicial interpretation of the impact of the Accord on the Charter of Rights and Freedoms". They go on to ask for the assurance that an intent not to harm the Charter is clear in the words of this historic Accord. Surely the First Ministers, the Government, and all Members of the House would agree that we do not know that this will happen, but we must deal with the concern that it may affect 52 per cent of the population.
My colleague who sat on the constitutional committee requested both the Prime Minister and the Minister responsible for the status of women that funding be made available from the federal Government, and that all possible support be given by the provinces and the federal Government to the proposed women's constitutional conference. It would present another opportunity for experts to consider all sides of the question.
It has been very difficult for groups to achieve a consensus in the form of one conclusive amendment. While we have proposed the inclusion of Section 28 of the Charter as an
Royal Assent
amendment, this would help reaffirm equality rights beyond a doubt.
There may be further suggestions from such a constitutional conference. I urge the Government and First Ministers to support this request and facilitate it. I also strongly urge the First Ministers not only to consider but to accept and implement the recommendations that were referred to earlier. If any group must not be left out, it is certainly the native people.
We support the primary objective of this Accord, which is to bring Quebec into the Constitution of Canada. While we support that objective strongly and joyfully, we cannot agree that this should be done with any diminution of rights for other people. That is why we believe that a constitutional conference for women should be supported.
I urge First Ministers to agree to amend the Accord as we have recommended and as a women's conference may recommend so that aboriginal people, northerners, minorities and women can have no further doubt that their rights will also be fully protected under our Constitution and Charter of Rights.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows that one of her colleagues from Vancouver was stripped of his responsibilities in the New Democratic Party because he is voting against the Accord. Does she agree with her leader on that action?

I do not know how my colleague from Vancouver will vote on the constitutional Accord. We have not yet voted. I certainly support my leader in almost everything he does. However, I think people have a right to their own opinions.

Mr. Speaker, given that the NDP has been quite critical in the past of the divisions and different positions in the Liberal caucus with respect to Meech Lake, I would like to ask the Hon. Mr. Speaker, I understand why these questions are being asked, of course. But as far as the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) is concerned I think it is important, as surely the Hon. Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member from Vancouver characterizes me as childish. There is one thing I can say. It is that within the Liberal Party, unlike the jackboot treatment of the NDP, we permit our members and our leaders to express a number of views without necessarily squashing them by stripping them of caucus responsibilities, et cetera.
Frankly, I found it rather astonishing to hear the Leader of the New Democratic Party say that he was issuing a special dispensation to the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) so that she could vote against the Meech Lake Accord when everyone else in his Party is being forced to toe the Party line for fear of being stripped of their responsibilities. Indeed, it has been a difficult struggle for us in the Liberal Party in terms of issues and positions. I know the NDP has been very vociferous in pointing out the divisions that exist in our Party. Those divisions do exist. I think the speeches that have been made in the House are testimony to that.
I believe that there are divisions internally in the Conservative Party, as there are in the New Democratic Party, which have been characterized in recent days by statements by various NDP Members that they will vote against the Accord. I cannot imagine how the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) could go across the country and say that he supports the Accord in every single province and the territories, except the Yukon, when he will allow one of his Members to take a postion different from the position of his Party simply to win an election. Either he believes in it or he does not believe in it. Either the Party believes in it or it does not believe in it.
If it is the position of the leader that he is in favour of Meech Lake, then how can he say in the context of the House of Commons that one single Member will have a dispensation? Is a new Member of Parliament in a better position to represent her constituents than is a Member who has been around for a while? Should we start discriminating just because someone happens to win an election?
It was unfathomable to me that the Leader of the NDP would make that type of statement when he knew full well that the intention of the Hon. Member for Yukon was simply to get elected. If she is going to come here and vote against the Meech Lake Accord singly and solely, it is obvious that the Accord will pass. I think it would have been far more honest of the Leader of the New Democratic Party to say, as has the Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner), that there are divisions in the NDP caucus, divisions based on regional concerns and of ethnicity and based on other concerns as opposed to the approach which he has taken. He has stated, instead, that he will offer dispensation similar, presumably, to what comes from the Pope in Rome. The Leader of the New Democratic Party will offer dispensation to a single Member and everyone else is supposed to fall in line. I think it is about time that the people of Canada started to recognize that.
October 8, 1987

I have heard, for example, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) make a very strong speech today in favour of the inclusion of women.
I know that the NDP will be sending out speeches across the country talking about all the wonderful things it will do to have women included in the Constitution. However, it seems to me that at least in the Liberal Party-and it has been a very tough time for us this last number of weeks-our leader is prepared to say that there is a variance of view, that there is a divergence of view, and that in the context of our Party and our caucus we will allow a full debate of all issues surrounding Meech Lake.
For me as a Liberal and as a Canadian it has been a very difficult experience to explore the number of issues surrounding Meech Lake. I think in particular of the exclusion of our aboriginal peoples. I think in particular of the concerns relating to provincial spending powers and how they might be applied on a national basis. I think in particular of the concerns expressed in my community about the possibility that we are relegating our multicultural groups to a second-class status.
However, I also think that in the context of the Meech Lake Accord the overriding belief of Canadians that when the Government of Quebec and the people of Quebec, in particular, said "Yes" to Canada, they said it because they believed that they were on the start of a new road to federalism. They said "Yes" because they thought they would see a follow-up from the referendum which would include a recognition of the distinct society in the Province of Quebec.
I believe on balance that Meech Lake has actually achieved the objective of the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society, and I embrace that particular recognition. As a Canadian and as a Liberal I am not afraid of the distinct society clause.
I think one of the joys of our country is that we have been able to embrace our differences and to celebrate our differences. We have been able, in the course of our history, to embrace multicultural groups, to embrace francophones and anglophones, and to bring people together.

Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to work in the Province of Quebec more than 12 years ago. That was the time when the Parti Quebecois was in opposition against the Liberals, a time when the people of Quebec were experiencing what was called the "quiet revolution". And I could see for myself that my Quebec friends, men and women alike, did live in a distinct society which had evolved over a few centuries, a society which was still in evolution despite certain religious standards, despite the legislative standards of the Canadian government, or despite the standards of religious groups in the Province of
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Quebec. Things have changed since the time when the first francophones came to settle in Canada. And to me it is important, as a country-
I can still vividly remember the night of the referendum when everybody-even in the riding of Hamilton East where there are not many francophones-was watching television, waiting-I was not feeling very well myself as I waited for the referendum results. At that time I was extremely pleased when Quebec, with its distinct society and its distinct character, with its history and its French culture, chose Canada. I was very glad as a Canadian.
But unfortunately, at the time I think a good many anglophones thought: Well, fine, that is the end of the francophonie chapter. Now we can deal with other problems. That is exactly what happened when Quebec refused to sign the Constitution.
Canada was not Canada without Quebec in the Constitution. And I think that the Meech Lake or Langevin Accord, with all the amendments made to try and accomodate changes in financing, jurisdictional issues and what not, means that Canada, for the first time, says yes to Quebecers.
Mr. Speaker, if Canadians are open-minded enough to be able to say yes to the distinct society in Quebec and do it wholeheartedly, I think this Government should be just as open-minded for our native people and for Canadian women who are concerned because, according to certain legal opinions, this Accord may affect their equality rights.
If, as a member of this House, I try and have an open mind and be receptive to this notion of distinct society in Quebec, I suggest that we should have this same attitude toward minority groups in other provinces.
The majority in Quebec managed to survive for 200 or 300 years despite the invasion of foreign media, and of English or American radio and television. You did survive. All we are asking for is that the same opportunity be given to minorities outside Quebec. Unfortunately, if the Liberal amendments are not accepted, especially those concerning the promotion of cultures, and the promotion of minorities outside Quebec . . . You all know that the 10 Premiers, and I know some of them, were willing to recognize the distinctiveness of Quebec and the rights of minorities in Quebec. But they were not all willing to accept the same rights for the minorities outside Quebec.
It is for that reason that no consensus could be found regarding promotion of culture for the minorities outside Quebec. It is sad to see that, as a Parliament, we are willing, even glad, to accept the distinct character of Quebec, but opposed to protection of minority rights in other provinces. Why is it so? Even the Government of Quebec and Mr. Bourassa, I believe, think that accepting amendments would somehow contribute to a reduction of rights. I believe, and that

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
is the way I tried to live my life, that respecting and even promoting the differences between people in no way reduces our own rights. We are not a society like the American one, where everybody should be the same, should drive a car and keep up with the Jones. We are not like that. After the battle of the Plains of Abraham the decision of our soldiers to let the vanquished practise their religion and use their language started a new society. That is in fact the way the distinct society started. After that, we constantly had forces in our country who wished to make French disappear.
I know that even in Hamilton changes over the last 10 years have been tremendous. We can see students lining up till midnight to register their children in schools where they will be able to learn French, a fact which attests to extraordinary changes over the last 10 of 15 years. So I think the people and the mentality have changed, there is greater openness, less fear, due to the fact that anglophones and francophones better understand and know one another, whether that is on account of the quiet revolution or the referendum that forced us in the anglophone community to face a new reality in Quebec. All we in the Liberal Party ask for is that Members of Parliament be prepared not only to ally the fears in Quebec as far as the francophone community is concerned, but similarly outside Quebec. I know the Government will echo the words of its legal advisors and say: "We will look after the aboriginal people at the next conference; as to women, do not worry, there is no problem. There is no problem either with multicul-turalism, because we will make appointments to some commissions or other." Unfortunately, to bring Quebec back as an equal partner, we have no choice. We must accept the Meech-Langevin Accord, pass it. At the same time, I think that we missed what could have been a real challenge for the Canadian Parliament because we could not widen our spectrum enough to be able to consider the first inhabitants of our country, our native people. We are not ready to consider the concern of women who really had to fight hard when the Constitution was written to get an equality rights clause that some premiers rejected. We know who they are, and at least one of them was trounced out of power because of his decision to drop the equality rights for women.
We proposed some amendments, on Senate reform for example. It is ironic, Mr. Speaker, because the Prime Minister frequently tells us in this House that the Senate is only a bunch of Liberal bagmen he would rather do away with. Now, the Liberal Party proposed an amendment which says that in the future the Senate will be elected, and that has been our policy since the last Liberal Party Congress in November, 1986. We should also note that it is supposed to be the policy of several Conservative Premiers, in particular the one from Alberta. We now have the opportunity, through some amendments, to start with an elected Senate: Why not agree to that change since the present Senate has often driven Conservative Members and even the Prime Minister himself to talk about its abolition. Unfortunately, because of the decision to reject any
kind of amendment, "possibly" because some Premiers might not accept them, the Parliament and the Prime Minister leave us with an agreement which is an improvement over what we presently have, but which is not what we could have had in the circumstances. Even if I admit that some Premiers might "possibly" say that we cannot touch what has been agreed upon, the notwithstanding clause for example, there is nothing in our amendments which would prejudice the rights contained in our Charter. That isn't so hard. Everybody here believes in the Constitution and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. So why not accept an amendment that guarantees, once and for all, that any changes arising from the distinct society concept will not derogate from any of the rights guaranteed by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms? That isn't so difficult.
Unfortunately, the Government did not have the courage to proceed with such amendments, fearing they would be rejected by the provincial Premiers. Mr. Speaker, I think that is why many Members in the Conservative Party have trouble supporting the Accord in its present form, and not because they are against the distinct society concept. In fact, they embrace that concept as I do, as a Canadian. I realize it is an essential point and that whether or not we put it in the Constitution, the fact is there. It is a point that cannot be denied by anyone. However, since the Government has rejected native demands, has refused to consider women's concerns, and will not consider changes to protect the very essence of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, some of us on this side will not vote for the Langevin Accord in its present form. I intend to support the Accord. But in doing so, I make the same mental reservation made by Quebecers who voted for Canada in the referendum. They voted for Canada, that is to say, they said no to sovereignty-association. They said yes to Canada. They said yes "maybe" with some apprehension about what the future would bring, hoping that further measures would be passed by Parliament and the legislatures to protect their distinct society. And if that is done, I hope that all Governments in Canada will understand that to develop and create a society with no fear, we have to enjoy the differences between our multicultural groups, the differences between the sexes, the differences with the first Canadian community, the native people, and that the Government will consider the Langevin Accord whether it is accepted or not as the first step in the right direction. We feel it is not enough to create a Canada where everyone can live knowing that our differences and our common bond are acknowledged. With the Langevin Accord, the Canadian link is a fact but I think that to continue to celebrate our differences, whether we are a minority in Quebec, or a majority outside Quebec, or a majority in Quebec, many more amendments as suggested by our Party should be approved. I should like Messrs. Mulroney, Bourassa and other Premiers who have promised to amend the Constitution to try to attain the purpose put forward by the Liberal Party.
October 8, 1987

speechtext: I regret that I have to tell the Hon. Member that her time has expired. Debate. The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster)

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to say a few words on the resolution before the House today concerning the Meech Lake Accord. This issue has been with us for many months now but this debate will be winding up in a few more days.
It seems to me that this is an important and historic debate for the House. Some of us had a chance to be here for the debate back in the early 1980s when we made the historic amendments to the Constitution which patriated the Constitution and installed a Charter of Rights in the it. Those were very historic days. It was a time which a country like Canada could only go through once.
[DOT]	(1740)
British parliamentary law does not provide for a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Many of the countries which have adopted the British Commonwealth, Westminster system of government have adopted a Charter of Rights, and it certainly was an historical occasion when we in Canada adopted one.
The Meech Lake Accord builds on that achievement. It provides for the Province of Quebec to join the Constitution. Of course, as long as Quebec is left out of the Constitution, it is not whole. Quebec represents some 28 per cent to 30 per cent of the population of Canada. It has a special position in our country because of its language, its culture and its different laws which were put in place in 1867.
This debate is an important one. It flows from those conditions Premier Bourassa set down in 1986 for Quebec's joining the Constitution. Of course, a great deal of work was done on those conditions in 1986 by members of our Party, by government Members and by Premier Bourassa. There were negotiations across the country.
Premier Bourassa's conditions included the recognition of the distinctive character of Quebec. He wanted to see some input from the provinces in the appointment of Supreme Court judges. That is perhaps to be understood because the Supreme Court governs both provincial and federal law in Canada. Premier Bourassa wanted to see the Cullen-Couture agreement on immigration put into the Constitution and he wanted to retain the traditional veto which Quebec had had up until the 1982 constitutional amendments. As well, he wanted to see some limitation on the spending power in areas of provincial jurisdiction.
The Meech Lake Accord meets most of those requirements. There has been a great deal of debate over whether Quebec should be described as having a distinctive character or as being a distinctive society. What concerns many Canadians is
Constitution Amendment, 1987
that the Meech Lake Accord as it was presented to Parliament seemed to go way beyond those five provisions which Premier Bourassa had suggested. It seems to deal with areas relating to the Senate and it constitutionalizes the federal-provincial First Ministers' Meetings.
Those of us who have been around here for some time would eventually like to see an elected Senate which represents in a more democratic way the regions. The constitutionalization of federal-provincial conferences seems to make the Premiers the representatives of the regions forever and a day.
There are those in this House, certainly including members of the NDP and perhaps others, who want to see the Senate done away with. I personally do not think that that will ever happen. I do not think it can be done without the consent of the provincial Governments. Clearly the provincial Governments in the Maritimes and in the west are opposed to that. Therefore, I do not understand why the federal-provincial First Ministers' Meetings were constitutionalized. That has been done and, of course, how much they are used depends on the Prime Minister of the day.
There was a great deal of concern over the extension of the veto to the amendment of the Senate. Many provinces do not want to see an elected Senate. It is hard to imagine that we will see total unanimity for an elected Senate in Canada. The extension of the veto power on that issue is especially unfortunate at this time because of the tremendous drive that exists in western Canada for an elected Senate.
Certainly the meetings I have attended in Saskatchewan and Alberta have indicated to me that there is a strong desire there for an elected Senate and our Party, at its policy conference last November, passed a resolution calling for the establishment of an elected Senate. It is part of our Party's policy and we will certainly work toward that.
The rigidity which has been introduced by the Meech Lake Accord with regard to the establishment of new provinces or the extension of existing provinces to the territories was in my view an unnecessary clause. Of course, that has been emphasized by northern Members who are all opposing the Accord because of that unanimity provision.
I think there is always a danger in a federal-provincial meeting of this type which brought in the Meech Lake Accord. There are 10 Premiers, and everything else being equal, they would all just as soon have more power. It is really up to the federal Government to defend federal powers. In this case, it seems that so many things beyond the original conditions of Premier Bourassa have been given away by the federal Government. It is not clear to me exactly why so much was given away.
The Premiers will now nominate people for appointment to the Senate. Although I think many provincial Premiers are just as capable of nominating representatives to the Senate as anyone else, their view tends to be more the provincial view. I personally feel it is better that appointments come from the

October 8, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
federal level where there is a national point of view. That is why our Party has put forward an amendment suggesting that on an interim basis until we have a fully elected Senate, we elect new Senators rather than have them nominated by the provincial Governments which tend to nominate people who have provincial points of view rather than the national point of view.
As I said, the Accord goes far beyond the original request of Premier Bourassa. The over-all tendency is toward the decentralization of power. Important changes were made at the second meeting of the First Ministers in that there would be no change in the federal and provincial powers under Section 91 and Section 92 of the Constitution Act. That tends to ensure that the power of those two levels of Government is not changed by the Accord, but the over-all tendency is toward greater decentralization and a greater rigidity in the Constitution. That is why we have moved our amendments.
For example, instead of the unanimity clause we would have the requirement of seven provinces representing 50 per cent of the population for the establishment of new provinces or changes to the Senate.
The other amendment which I feel is quite important is the provision of a national standard for federal spending in areas of provincial jurisdiction. We probably will not have many more new social programs such as the Canada Pension Plan or medicare or the Canada Assistance Program, but who knows. At some time in the future we may have a guaranteed income program. We may have agricultural programs which will meet the new standards of the OECD.
Where provinces opt out of national programs, the Liberal Party believes that not only should that province establish a compatible program, but one with a minimum standard equivalent to that provided by the federal Government. Certainly in the Langevin discussions there seemed to be a provision that those standards would be national standards, but for greater certainty we would like to see the amendment we have put forward adopted by the House.
That brings up the whole question of amendments. Clearly, this is an extremely undemocratic procedure that we are going through. There have been two all-night meetings where the Premiers were locked up with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and a deal was hammered out. That deal was brought to the floor of this House with the Government saying we will have discussions and public hearings but we will not accept amendments. I hope we never have that kind of a constitutional amendment again. It is simply not in keeping with the way you govern a democratic country like ours. It is an extremely backward step. That is why we put forward our amendments. We know the Government will vote them down but that is not the last word. There are provincial Governments which will deal with this, I believe in a more democratic fashion. If they adopt some of the amendments we are putting
forward, which we believe are more democratic, less rigid and more desirable, we would welcome it back to this House. In any event, I certainly hope that when constitutional amendments are next adopted it is done on a more democratic basis.
The fact that the Government has not provided constitutional amendments to deal with aboriginal problems is a gross blunder and great disappointment. Not only the native people but the people of the North are severely grieved by this document. Our amendments provide greater certainty that the rights of native people and women will not be overridden by this Accord. We would also like to see an amendment relating to the multicultural nature of our country. I do not for the life of me know why the Government has not adopted that amendment. I hope one of the provincial Governments will, so that the multicultural nature, which you, Mr. Speaker, and so many others represent in this House, will be fully recognized in the Constitution.
Despite all the problems I have outlined with this Accord, we still come down to the basic question of whether we want to adopt it now or wait for another day to see Quebec in the Constitution. My belief is that with all the difficulties, and I hope some of them will be corrected, if not by this Government then by one of the provincial Governments, it is important that this matter be dealt with now. We have a federalist Liberal Premier in Quebec with a Party in a strong position to work out a deal. It is not the deal we want but it will bring Quebec into the Constitution. It means we can go forward as a nation. Therefore I hope the Accord will be adopted, in amended form if possible. However, we should not miss this opportunity to make Canada whole by seeing Quebec become a part of the Constitution.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I would like to co-operate with the Chair as usual. It is six o'clock and I just want to make sure that we all understand the point made by the Government House Leader and that the next discussion of Meech Lake will be on Monday, unless of course unpredictable circumstances arise.
I would like to make it clear on the record that that will be the case unless an unpredictable event takes place. I just want to make sure that we will still have the floor for the 10-minute question and comment period.
