AIR TRANSPORT-PROPOSED TRANSPORTATION OF PLUTONIUM THROUGH CANADIAN AIRSPACE/TERRITORIAL SOVEREIGNTY
['The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly this House stands adjourned until tomorrow at 10 a.m., pursuant to Standing Order 3(1).']

Mr. Speaker, on August 21 I asked the Government what it was doing to ensure that reprocessed plutonium would not be flown from Japan to France across Canada's north. I was told to be reassured that the Government would be acting in the best interests of Canadians. I and many other Canadians do not find that reassuring as we watch what the Government is currently doing in some of our other best interests.
I would like to point out that 1 was not the first to raise this question. On March 24, March 31, August 11, August 13, August 17 and August 28 Hon. Members asked the Government for some answers and received such reassurances as "well, no one has asked us formally and when they do we will respond", "we'll do the right thing", and the most insightful answer from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), "relax".
I hope that you, Mr. Speaker, and other Canadians will feel relaxed knowing that, first, according to current information, the plutonium will be in such a fine particle state that one speck inhaled will be carcinogenic. Two, the composition of the particles is such that they would be suspended in the air if they were released. Therefore, in the event of a crash or mid-air explosion it would be absolutely impossible to clean up.
Three, standards for casks capable of withstanding either a mid-air explosion or a crash which are currently set by international standards are set on the basis of impact at 30 miles per hour. I do not think the planes will be flying over Canada at 30 miles an hour.
Five, the plutonium which will be transported will be of such a toxicity that its toxicity will be increased by 60 per cent over several decades. There will be a legacy for our children and our children's children should there be a spill.
Adjournment Debate
Six, the agreement proposed between the U.S. and Japan is for 30 years. The U.S. Nuclear Energy Institute states that it will take one flight every two weeks over a period of 10 years in order to transport this plutonium to Japan from France. On each flight there will be enough plutonium to make 15 to 20 bombs, each the size of the Nagasaki bomb. It is important to note that the plutonium is in such a chemical state that any high school student could easily and readily make a bomb.
Now that you are relaxed after having heard these facts, Mr. Speaker, let me tell you about some people who are not relaxed. Certainly John Polanyi, Nobel prize winner, has expressed his concerns. He said that should there be a spill, the environmental hazards both to persons and the environment will last for thousands of years.
The State of Alaska is also concerned. It is currently suing the United States federal Government over the issue and is calling for a full environmental assessment review.
In addition to those concerns, there have been articles in newspapers throughout the country, including the Vancouver Sun, La Presse, Le Devoir, The Globe and Mail, the Winnipeg Free Press and the Windsor Free Press. Editorials throughout the country have stated that the Government should have dealt with the issue since it was first raised in March.
I want to summarize the three areas of concern. The first is the obvious environmental hazard in the event of a crash or mid-air collision. Second, should we allow these flights when there is a potential contribution to nuclear proliferation in the event of a hijacking. The third issue is sovereignty. Will the Government simply accept this proposal without the appropriate early intervention? Will the Government allow the United States to fly over northern Canada, which, incidentally, has been suggested as a route because it is uninhabited? That will be a big surprise to the people who live there. There is an alternate route across New York and Washington, D.C., but that does not appear to be a route being contemplated.
Other Members of the House have tried to bring these concerns to the Government, but without satisfaction. Daily I receive letters about this issue from my constituents and residents of the Northwest Territories, Ontario and other provinces.
Will the Government finally take some action and state an unequivocal no to this suicidal scheme? Will it take action now before the President and Congress ratify this agreement? Will it undertake the common sense solution and propose that Japan build its own reprocessing facilities?

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin), I can only reiterate assurances already provided by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on numerous occasions in the House.

October 8, 1987
Adjournment Debate
First and foremost, I would emphasize that while a draft agreement has been negotiated between the United States and Japan, it has not yet been signed. No decisions on the potential routing of these shipments have been made at this time. Indeed, it may all be hypothetical as other routes are certainly possible.
If and when an agreement is signed, however, I again remind Hon. Members that the movement of all dangerous goods by air is subject to both an international convention and domestic legislation.
In the international arena, Canada is a signatory nation of the International Civil Aviation Organization and as such has a number of options available. We can request that prenotification be given and that approval be received prior to any overflight being undertaken. In this case we would insist that the most stringent requirements for safe packaging be met as well as all safety and inspection requirements. As well, we can deny any overflight by filing a state variance with the International Civil Aviation Organization based on Canada's concern with any inadequate safety measures of such flights.
This Government has made representation to the United States Government in May and August of 1986 and again in April of this year, expressing our deep concerns in this matter. We have also spoken to Japan about the same concern.
This Government is monitoring the situation very closely. The permission of the Canadian Government would be required on a case-by-case basis before any such overflights could take place. I can assure Hon. Members that no such overflights would be carried out without our express approval. Canadian safety standards are among the highest in the world and any proposal would be fully scrutinized to ensure that these high standards are fully complied with, particularly in the area of safe packaging. Any decision taken by this Government would make the safety of Canada and Canadians the most important consideration.

subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF CERTAIN POSTAL SERVICES-PROVISION OF SERVICE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
CANADA POST CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF CERTAIN POSTAL SERVICES-PROVISION OF SERVICE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
On May
21, 1987, Mr. Speaker, I directed the following question to the Minister responsible for Canada Post: Why is he doing everything he can to stop the postal service?
When the Canada Post Corporation was created by Parliament in 1981, Mr. Speaker, its mandate included the following: Firstly, to improve the postal service; secondly, to improve its industrial relations; and thirdly, to reduce its deficit.
Since then it has lived up to its mandate. It has substantially reduced its deficit. It was improving relations with its employees to the point that we had had no strike since 1981;
the first one occurred in May 1987, and now, three months later, we are faced with a second strike. Mr. Speaker, even if Canada Post had been slower to improve its service, slower than with the other two parts of its mandate, it did improve its service.
We should not forget that we had been faced with nearly 20 years of conflicts at the time the Corporation was a department. We could not expect some 20 years of conflicts to be forgotten overnight. It will take a number of years. Therefore, we were making progress.
But in February, 1986, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance clearly indicated in his Budget that effective March 31, 1988, Canada Post would have to become self-financed, meaning that it would have to operate at a profit, for the Federal Government would no longer soak up its deficit.
That is when our problems started, Mr. Speaker, for Canada Post turned around and said: Well, we are going to fulfil our mandate, present a corporate plan which the Government will accept and we are going to balance our books. And that is what happened, Mr. Speaker. This corporate plan provides for two systems of postal delivery in this country: one is home delivery of mail, which had been the general custom in Canada until then, and the other is delivery of mail to superboxes.
Since that plan was tabled, I can assure you that many communities have had neither door-to-door delivery nor temporary green boxes or superboxes, and many thousands of Canadians have to get their mail once a week, because they are away at work and cannot always drop in at the post office.
The current situation is unacceptable, Mr. Speaker. Now, after all those fights, those negotiations, the Government stands behind Canada Post-the Government gave that mandate to balance the books by March 31, 1988-and labour relations have been deteriorating. When Canada Post was established, we even appointed labour representatives to the Board of Directors of Canada Post in order to create a link, a work relation, in order that they might themselves take part in the management of the corporation and become aware of the difficulties-to create a climate of understanding.
However, Mr. Speaker, in-fighting has set-in. The Government has replaced those people. The situation now is that the Government has hired strike-breakers during the strike last May.
In 1987, a government that allows its own corporations . . . We are the shareholders of that corporation, Mr. Speaker. The Government as shareholder allows Canada Post to hire strikebreakers, to provoke violence in the workplace, and last May after many requests to appoint a mediator immediately, to solve that problem, the Government took 10 days, then the mediator needed only two days to solve the problem. This time, Mr. Speaker, we are not solving the problem. The strike has been on for a week, but the Government does not want to appoint a mediator. And now back-to-work legislation has
October 8, 1987

been introduced-so much for our collective agreement settlement procedure.
You are signaling that my time has expired. I should like to conclude by reading two paragraphs of the October 2, Halifax Chronicle-Herald editorial.
Privatization has brought us to the current strike situation. Neither side is yet prepared to back away from their fixed positions. That is understandable in the sense that what is at issue is the future capability of the Canadian postal system.
We doubt that either a national strike or back-to-work legislation will help much to attain that goal. It might be more helpful, however, if the post office Act is amended to more fully define the nature of the postal service and to blend the many views of what such service is and how it is to be provided.

Mr. Speaker, time has come for a new debate so we might at last define what kind of postal service we want to offer Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADA POST CORPORATION-REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF CERTAIN POSTAL SERVICES-PROVISION OF SERVICE-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Post Office in Canada has a long and proud history. Canadians were proud to receive mail from Canada Post in its former shape. As well, people were proud to work for Canada Post. However, in recent years there is no doubt that they came upon hard times and problems. As times changed, as management changed, and as unions changed, it led to problems.
A particular problem was that past Governments interfered in the operation of the Post Office. The result was that

management could not manage and unions could not work for the workers. We faced the situation of unions actually trying to manage the Post Office. That just cannot work. Managers must manage.
Parliament tried a number of experiments to see what would work. The most recent one when the Hon. Member's Party was in Government was to create a separate Crown corporation. That has worked. Now, under the new President, Mr. Donald Lander, there is a postal corporate plan. I have looked at the plan and I have gone to briefings on it until I have been blue in the face. The plan is clear. Management changes have been made, because not all the faults were union faults. Working place changes have been made. It has clear goals in respect of service and independent auditing and checking of those goals.
I have absolutely no doubt that there is better postal service today than there was six months ago, 12 months ago, or 18 months ago. If we stick with the plan and let management manage and unions do what they are supposed to do in terms of their job, I can tell the Hon. Member opposite that we will be very proud of the result. I have no doubt that within a year or so Canadians can be once again proud of the Post Office, and people who work for the Post Office can be proud to say that they work for Canada Post.
